lead: In this white week the Church keeps returning to one truth from different sides: death has been answered. Hebrews takes up Psalm 8, which marvels that God crowned human beings with glory, and admits that we do not yet see everything under their feet, “but we do see Jesus”. In the Gospel some Sadducees bring Jesus a puzzle meant to make the resurrection look absurd, and he answers that God “is God not of the dead, but of the living”. One reading shows the risen Lord crowned; the other shows why that crown is meant for us too.

r.h: We do see Jesus, crowned with glory
set: Hebrews is a sermon in written form, which its author calls a “word of exhortation” (13:22). The author does not give his name. The early Church already discussed whether it was Paul's, and Origen said that only God knows who wrote it; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Chapter 1 has shown the Son far above the angels. Chapter 2 now asks why, then, he was made lower than them for a time.

To answer, the author quotes Psalm 8 from the Greek Bible. The psalm speaks of humanity in general: the small human being whom God has crowned and set over creation. The author notices that this is not what we see now. Then he finds one human being in whom the psalm has already come true.
str: v. 5: the world to come is not placed under angels.
vv. 6–8a: Psalm 8: what are human beings, that you are mindful of them?
v. 8b: we do not yet see everything subject to them,
v. 9: but we see Jesus, lowered for a little while, crowned because of the suffering of death, tasting death for everyone.
kw: Literally “the inhabited world to come”. It is the new creation that began when Christ rose and entered glory. The author adds “about which we are speaking”, because the whole sermon is about it.
a little, for a little while

The Hebrew of Psalm 8 says that God made human beings a little lower than ’elōhîm, “God” or “heavenly beings”, and the Greek translators wrote “angels”. The Greek phrase can mean “a little” in rank or “for a little while” in time. Hebrews uses the second sense: the Son was lower than the angels only for the short time of his earthly life and death.
A Semitic way of saying “experience death”. It does not mean a small sip. He went all the way into death, and he did it “for everyone”.
vv: What are human beings that you are mindful of them, or mortals, that you care for them?

The Greek has “man” and “son of man”, which NRSV renders as “human beings” and “mortals”. Christian readers have long heard in “son of man” the title Jesus used of himself. The author lets both senses stand: Jesus is the true man in whom the calling of all humanity is fulfilled.
As it is, we do not yet see everything in subjection to them,
An honest sentence. The author does not pretend that the world already looks redeemed. Death, sickness and injustice are still here.
but we do see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death,
This is the first time the sermon uses the name Jesus, and it comes at the high point. The crown is not given in spite of the suffering but “because of” it.
so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.

A few ancient witnesses read “apart from God” instead of “by the grace of God”, and Origen already knew both readings. The two phrases look alike in Greek (chariti theou, chōris theou). The best manuscripts and almost all translations have “by the grace of God”, and that is the reading the Church proclaims.
ch: The Catechism cites this verse when it teaches that Jesus Christ tasted death for the benefit of every human being, and that it was truly the Son of God made man who died and was buried (CCC 629). The Second Vatican Council teaches that Christ, the new Adam, fully reveals man to himself and makes his high calling clear (Gaudium et Spes 22). So the psalm's question, “What are human beings?”, finds its full answer in the risen Lord. His glory is not a prize for a stranger; it is the first fruit of our own.

r.h: God of the living
set: Jesus is in the Temple at Jerusalem in the last days before his Passion. One group after another comes to question him: the chief priests, scribes and elders about his authority (11:27–33), then Pharisees and Herodians about the tax (12:13–17), and now Sadducees. This is the only time they appear in Mark's Gospel.

The Sadducees were a priestly and wealthy party, closely linked with the Temple. They held to the written law of Moses and did not accept the traditions that the Pharisees taught, and they denied the resurrection of the dead (see Acts 23:8). Their question rests on the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–10: a brother was to marry the widow of a man who died without a son, so that the dead man's name would not be blotted out in Israel.
str: vv. 18–23: the Sadducees' case: seven brothers and one wife.
v. 24: Jesus' answer: you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God.
v. 25: the power of God: the risen do not marry.
vv. 26–27: the scriptures: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God of the living.
kw: Literally “standing up again”. In verse 23 the Sadducees use it as a trap, but it is the word of Easter.
From planaō, to wander or go astray; our word “planet”, a wandering star, comes from the same root. Jesus uses it at the beginning and at the end of his answer (vv. 24, 27), like a frame.
The Sadducees pictured the life to come as this life carried on, and so it looked absurd. Jesus says that God's power makes something new.
vv: Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?
Two failures, and Jesus answers each in turn: the power of God in verse 25, the scriptures in verses 26 and 27.
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
The risen do not become angels. They share the angels' undying life, and so marriage, which carries life forward through children, has finished its earthly task. Love itself is not lost.
He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.

God spoke to Moses at the bush long after the patriarchs had died (Exodus 3:6), and he still called himself their God. A bond with God is not ended by death. Those whom God has made his own are kept alive in him.
ch: The Catechism quotes this answer when it teaches that Jesus firmly taught the resurrection of the dead (CCC 993), and then adds that he binds faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25; CCC 994). What Jesus argued in the Temple, he showed at the tomb. The patriarchs, the martyrs and our own beloved dead live to God, and every Holy Qurbono is offered in communion with them.

qa: Will husband and wife know each other in heaven?

Jesus does not say that the bonds of this life are forgotten. He says that marriage, as an institution of this age with its task of bringing children into the world, belongs to this age. The Catechism describes heaven as the perfect life with the Holy Trinity, a communion of life and love with the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed (CCC 1024). Every true love that was lived in God is purified and fulfilled there, not erased.
study: The Sadducees' puzzle tried to make faith look foolish. How do I answer, gently and clearly, when someone mocks the hope of the resurrection?
“We do not yet see everything in subjection.” Where do I find it hard to believe that Christ has already won? What would help me to “see Jesus” there?

lead: The Friday of Hevoro week is kept as the commemoration of all the Confessors, the faithful who bore witness to Christ before others, many of them to the point of death. Hebrews runs out of time to name such people: judges, kings and prophets, and countless unnamed men and women “of whom the world was not worthy”. In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples three times not to be afraid, because the Father counts even the hairs of their heads, and he promises to acknowledge before the Father everyone who acknowledges him. The Church reads these together in Easter week because the resurrection is what makes such courage reasonable.

r.h: Of whom the world was not worthy
set: Chapter 11 is a long roll of honour that begins with a definition: “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1). Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and others follow, each introduced with the words “by faith”. Our reading is the end of the list, where the author speeds up because the names are too many.

The sermon was written for Christians who had already suffered public abuse, prison and the loss of their property (10:32–34), and who were growing tired. The heroes of Israel are set before them as companions in the same race (12:1).
str: v. 32: names without stories: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.
vv. 33–35a: what faith achieved: victories, rescues, the dead given back.
vv. 35b–38: what faith endured: torture, prison, stoning, the sword, exile.
vv. 39–40: none of them received what was promised, so that they might be made perfect together with us.
kw: The phrase sums up the whole list. Faith here is trust in God's promise that holds on when the promise is not yet seen.

The verb comes from the word for a drum, and seems to mean a beating or torture on a frame. 2 Maccabees 6:19 and 6:28 use the related noun for the instrument to which the old man Eleazar went of his own accord rather than betray the law.

A favourite word of Hebrews: to be brought to completion, to reach the goal. Christ himself was made “perfect through sufferings” (2:10), and through him the saints of the old covenant reach the goal together with us.
vv: Women received their dead by resurrection.
The widow of Zarephath through Elijah (1 Kings 17:17–24) and the Shunammite woman through Elisha (2 Kings 4:18–37). Those were returns to this life, which would end again.
Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.

The “better resurrection” is the one that never ends. The author is thinking of the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, the old man Eleazar and the mother with her seven sons, who died hoping that the King of the universe would raise them “to an everlasting renewal of life” (2 Maccabees 7:9).
they were sawn in two,

Scripture does not tell this story. An ancient Jewish tradition, preserved in the writing known as the Ascension of Isaiah, held that the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, and many think that the author has this in mind.
of whom the world was not worthy.
A reversal. The world judged these people unfit and drove them out to deserts and caves. God's judgement is that the world was unfit for them.
since God had provided something better so that they would not, apart from us, be made perfect.
The saints of Israel are not left behind. Their hope and ours are fulfilled together, in Christ, in one family.
ch: The Church honours the holy men and women of the Old Testament as our fathers and mothers in faith; the Catechism calls Abraham “the father of all who believe” (CCC 146). It also teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The mother and her seven sons of 2 Maccabees are honoured in the calendars of many Churches, East and West, a sign that the Church knows this cloud of witnesses to be one.

r.h: Do not be afraid; acknowledge me
set: Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in Matthew's Gospel, the one in which Jesus sends out the Twelve. He tells them plainly that they will be handed over to councils and brought before governors and kings because of him (10:17–18), and that a disciple is not above his teacher (10:24). Our verses come right after, and three times they say “do not fear” (vv. 26, 28, 31).
str: vv. 26–27: what is hidden will be revealed; proclaim it from the housetops.
v. 28: fear God, not those who can kill only the body.
vv. 29–31: the sparrows and the hairs of your head: you are of more value.
vv. 32–33: acknowledging and denying.
kw: Literally “to say the same thing”, to agree openly and publicly. It is the word behind the Church's “confession” of faith, and a confessor is one who has made that confession under trial. Matthew's Greek says, in a Semitic turn of phrase, “confess in me”.

A small Roman copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius, when a denarius was a labourer's daily wage. Two sparrows cost that much. In Luke five sparrows are sold for two pennies (Luke 12:6), and preachers like to say that the fifth was thrown in for nothing, yet God does not forget it.
The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, remembered for the evil once done there (Jeremiah 7:31). In Jesus' words it stands for final ruin, the loss of body and soul together.
vv: What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.
The flat roofs of a village were where news was called out. The quiet teaching given to a few is meant for the whole world.
rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
This is God, not the devil. Fear of God here is not terror but reverence, taking God seriously, and it drives out every lesser fear.
And even the hairs of your head are all counted.
A care that reaches to what no one else would bother to count.
Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
The word “therefore” ties the promise to the sparrows: because the Father cares, the disciple can speak. Jesus will speak for us as we have spoken for him.
ch: The Catechism cites this saying when it teaches that those who belong to Christ through faith and Baptism must confess their baptismal faith before others (CCC 14). Peter, who denied the Lord three times, was restored by the risen Christ and later gave his life for him (John 21:15–19). For anyone who returns, denial is not the last word.

rite: Our West Syriac tradition fills the days of Hevoro week with the joy of the Resurrection, and on this Friday it remembers all the Confessors, the men and women who confessed Christ before others by their life and often by their death. Many of their names are known only to God. The Malankara Church keeps this day in thanksgiving for them, from the first centuries to our own time, and in prayer for all who suffer for their faith in many lands today, and for those who make them suffer.
study: Where am I tempted to keep my faith “in the dark”, at work, among friends or online? What would it mean to acknowledge Christ there, simply and kindly?
Which confessor of the faith, from the Scriptures, the saints or my own family, gives me courage? What did that person fear less than I do?

lead: Hebrews calls Jesus “the apostle and high priest of our confession” and compares him with Moses: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant, Christ over it as a son, “and we are his house”. In the Gospel the apostle John wants to stop a man who drives out demons in Jesus' name because he is not one of their group, and Jesus says, “Do not stop him.” Both readings are about the household of God: who builds it, who belongs to it, and how wide its doors are.

r.h: Faithful as a son over God's house
set: Hebrews has just called Jesus “a merciful and faithful high priest” (2:17). Now the author takes up the word “faithful” and sets Jesus beside Moses, the greatest figure in Israel's history. The comparison is made with deep respect for Moses. It rests on Numbers 12:7, where God defends Moses against Aaron and Miriam: “he is entrusted with all my house.”
str: v. 1: consider Jesus, apostle and high priest.
v. 2: he was faithful, as Moses was.
vv. 3–4: the builder and the house; God is the builder of all things.
vv. 5–6a: Moses as a servant in the house, Christ as a son over it.
v. 6b: we are his house, if we hold firm.
kw: This is the only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called an apostle. He is the one sent from God to us, and the priest who goes from us to God.
Both a building and a household, the family who live in it. Here it means God's people.
The word used of Moses in the Greek of Numbers 12:7. It is an honourable word for a trusted attendant, not a slave.
Literally “saying everything”, the boldness of one who has the right to speak. In Hebrews it is the confidence with which Christians may come before God (4:16; 10:19).
vv: consider that Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
“Confession” is homologia, the faith that the Church says aloud together, as in the Creed.
Yet Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.
Moses belongs to the house; he is one of its greatest members. Jesus belongs on the builder's side, with God, who builds all things (v. 4).
Christ, however, was faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house if we hold firm the confidence and the pride that belong to hope.
A gift and a condition. We are already the house. We remain so by holding on in hope.
ch: The Church calls herself the house of God, in which his family dwells (CCC 756). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial priesthood each share, in its own way, in the one priesthood of Christ (Lumen Gentium 10). Easter week, when the early Church welcomed the newly baptized, is a fitting time to remember that we are not visitors in this house but its living stones (1 Peter 2:5).

r.h: Do not stop him
set: This short exchange closes Jesus' ministry in Galilee in Luke's Gospel. Just before it the disciples argued about which of them was the greatest, and Jesus set a child beside him (9:46–48). In the next verse Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and John, with his brother James, will soon want to call down fire on a Samaritan village (9:54). Here John speaks for the group.
str: v. 49: John reports: we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
v. 50: Jesus: do not stop him; whoever is not against you is for you.
kw: To act in someone's name is to act with his authority and power. The man was calling on Jesus, and it worked.
The tense can describe an attempt: we kept trying to stop him. The same verb appears when Jesus says of the children, “do not stop them” (18:16).
vv: we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
The reason is revealing: not “he does not follow you”, but “he does not follow with us”. The disciples have mixed up loyalty to Jesus with belonging to their own circle.
Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.

Luke also records the other saying, “Whoever is not with me is against me” (11:23). The two do not contradict each other. One is about our own stand toward Christ, where there is no neutral ground; the other is about how we regard others who call on his name, where we should be generous.
ch: Moses gave the same answer when Joshua wanted to stop two men who were prophesying in the camp: “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29). The Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, gifts that belong to the Church of Christ and impel toward unity (Lumen Gentium 8; CCC 819). This is not indifference about the truth. It is joy wherever Christ's name is honoured, and a longing for full communion.

study: “We are his house.” What does it change in my week to think of my parish not as a building I visit but as a household I belong to?
When have I been slow to rejoice at good done by Christians outside my own group or Church? What would Jesus' “Do not stop him” ask of me?

lead: New Sunday closes the white week, and the Church sets a full table. The Evening Gospel (John 20:19–23) gives the first evening of Easter: “Peace be with you … Receive the Holy Spirit.” Four Old Testament lessons follow. Genesis 41:37–45 raises Joseph, once thrown into a pit, over all the land of Egypt. 2 Kings 2:1–12 shows Elijah taken up and Elisha asking for a double share of his spirit. Wisdom 3:1–9 says, “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God”. Isaiah 40:9–15 cries to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!” Then 1 Peter 1:3–12 blesses God who has given us “a new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead”.

We study three of these closely. The lesson from 2 Kings stands nearest to the Gospel: a master taken from his disciple, a condition about seeing, and a spirit handed on. Paul, a prisoner, tells Timothy to “remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead”. John brings us twice into the room with closed doors, and to Thomas, who will not believe until he sees, and then makes the fullest confession of faith in the Gospels. The line runs from Elisha's “if you see me” to the Lord's “Blessed are those who have not seen”, and its key words are spirit, remember and believe.

r.h: If you see me as I am being taken
set: Elijah the Tishbite was the great prophet of the northern kingdom in the ninth century before Christ, in the days of King Ahab. He stood alone against the worship of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18), and at Horeb he met the Lord not in wind, earthquake or fire but in “a sound of sheer silence” (1 Kings 19:12). There he was told to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place, and he threw his mantle over Elisha as he ploughed (1 Kings 19:16, 19).

Our reading is the handing over. The two men walk from Gilgal to Bethel, from Bethel to Jericho, and on to the Jordan. Each time Elijah tells Elisha to stay behind, and each time Elisha refuses. Groups of prophets watch, and they know what is coming. Readers have long noticed that the parting of the Jordan and the crossing on dry ground recall Israel's entry into the land under Joshua (Joshua 3).
str: vv. 1–6: three stages, three times “Stay here”, three times “I will not leave you”.
vv. 7–8: by the Jordan, the mantle strikes the water and it parts.
vv. 9–10: the request for a double share of the spirit, and its condition.
vv. 11–12: chariot and horses of fire; Elijah taken up; Elisha's cry and his torn clothes.
¶ The story's weight lies in faithfulness. Because Elisha refused three times to leave his master, he is there to see, and to receive.
kw: A storm wind. The Lord answered Job out of such a wind (Job 38:1). Elijah is taken up by the wind, while the chariot of fire separates the two men.

Literally “a mouth of two”, a portion of two. Deuteronomy 21:17 uses it for the inheritance of the firstborn son, who receives twice what each of the others receives. Elisha is not asking to be twice as great as Elijah. He is asking to be his heir, the firstborn among his disciples.
The prophet's cloak, the sign of his office. Elijah threw it over Elisha at his call, uses it here to strike the Jordan, and leaves it behind for him (2:13).
vv: As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.
An oath, repeated three times (vv. 2, 4, 6). Ruth said something like it to Naomi (Ruth 1:16–17). Faithfulness to the one who has taught you is the road to receiving his gift.
Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.
He asks for nothing else: no wealth, no title. The spirit is the Lord's gift that made Elijah a prophet.
if you see me as I am being taken from you, it will be granted you; if not, it will not.
Seeing is the condition. Elisha must keep his eyes on his master to the end. Today's Gospel also speaks of seeing, and then goes beyond it.
Father, father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!
Elisha calls Elijah “father”, as the disciples of a prophet did, and names him as Israel's true defence, worth more than an army. The same cry is raised over Elisha himself when he is dying (13:14).
ch: Israel remembered Elijah's going up with hope: Malachi promised that the Lord would send him again before the great day (Malachi 4:5), and Jesus said that Elijah had already come, meaning John the Baptist (Matthew 17:12–13). The Catechism calls Elijah the father of the prophets (CCC 2582). Christian readers from early times have seen in this scene a figure of the Lord's own going up to the Father and of the Spirit he gives to his disciples. The difference is as important as the likeness: Elijah was taken up; Christ rose and ascended by his own power, and with his own breath he gives the Spirit.

r.h: Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead
set: Second Timothy is written as Paul's last letter. He is a prisoner in Rome (1:17), many have deserted him (1:15), and he knows that his death is near (4:6). He writes to Timothy, his beloved “child”, who is leading the church at Ephesus. Many scholars today think that the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus) were written after Paul's death by a disciple in his name; others, with the long tradition of the Church, hold that they come from Paul himself. Either way the Church receives the letter as inspired Scripture, and its voice is that of the apostle facing death.
Monday's epistle takes up the second half of this passage again, so here we give more time to its opening verses.
str: v. 1: be strong in grace.
v. 2: hand on what you have heard, to faithful people who will teach others.
vv. 3–7: three pictures: the soldier, the athlete, the farmer.
vv. 8–10: remember Jesus Christ, raised; the word of God is not chained.
vv. 11–13: a sure saying, perhaps from an early hymn.
kw: A word for placing something valuable in the keeping of a trustworthy person. The faith is a deposit (1:12, 14) passed from hand to hand: from Paul to Timothy, to faithful people, and to others. Four generations of teaching appear in one verse.
A rare word that joins “with” to “suffer hardship”. In the New Testament it appears only in this letter (1:8; 2:3). Timothy is not asked to suffer alone, but alongside Paul and alongside Christ.
A present command: keep on remembering. Remembering here is not looking back with longing; it is keeping the living Lord before one's eyes.
vv: You then, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus;
Strength comes first from grace, not from willpower.
what you have heard from me through many witnesses entrust to faithful people who will be able to teach others as well.
A short picture of apostolic tradition. The Church's teaching is not invented anew in each generation. It is received, guarded and handed on.
And in the case of an athlete, no one is crowned without competing according to the rules.
The soldier teaches single-mindedness, the athlete discipline, the farmer patient work (vv. 4–6). All three wait for a reward that comes at the end.
Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David

The whole gospel in a line: raised from the dead, and of David's line, so truly human and truly the promised King. The Greek is a perfect participle: he is the one who has been raised and remains risen.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that, so that the Gospel might always be kept whole and alive in the Church, the apostles left bishops as their successors and handed over to them their own teaching office (Dei Verbum 7), and that what the apostles handed on includes everything that helps the People of God to live holily and to grow in faith (Dei Verbum 8). St Irenaeus taught that the tradition of the apostles can be found in every church by looking to the succession of bishops from the apostles (in substance). Timothy stands at the head of that chain.

r.h: My Lord and my God!
set: It is the evening of the first day of the week. That morning Mary Magdalene had found the tomb empty, had met the risen Lord, and had told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” (20:18). Yet they are behind locked doors, John says “for fear of the Jews”. In John's Gospel this phrase usually means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people, to whom Jesus and his disciples themselves belonged.

The scene comes in two parts, a week apart. Thomas, called the Twin, was absent the first time. He has spoken before in this Gospel: when Jesus decided to go to Bethany, he said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (11:16), and at the Supper he asked, “How can we know the way?” (14:5). He is brave, and he wants to understand.
str: vv. 19–20: the first evening: closed doors, peace, the wounds shown, joy.
vv. 21–23: the sending, the breath, the Spirit, the power to forgive.
vv. 24–25: Thomas absent, and his conditions.
vv. 26–27: eight days later the Lord meets Thomas's conditions.
vv. 28–29: Thomas's confession, and the blessing for those who have not seen.
¶ The two parts have the same shape: the doors are shut, Jesus stands among them, and he says, “Peace be with you.” His coming does not depend on our opening the door.
kw: The everyday greeting, shalom. On the risen Lord's lips it is the gift he promised at the Supper: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (14:27).

The same rare verb is used in the Greek Bible when God breathes the breath of life into the first human being (Genesis 2:7), and in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). This is the new creation.
The Greek word for “twin”. The name Thomas itself comes from the Aramaic word for twin, so the Gospel gives his name and then translates it.
ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou
The fullest confession of faith in the Gospels. The Gospel began with “the Word was God” (1:1), and now a disciple says it to the risen Jesus face to face.
vv: After he said this, he showed them his hands and his side.
The risen body keeps the wounds. They are not erased but glorified, the signs that the one standing here is the one who was crucified.
As the Father has sent me, so I send you.
Jesus' own mission becomes theirs. The Church is sent as he was sent.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.

The first gift of the risen Lord, together with the Spirit, is the power to forgive. The Council of Trent taught that these words are to be understood of the power of forgiving and retaining sins in the sacrament of Penance.
Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.
Thomas will not borrow someone else's faith. His demand is precise: he wants to know that the risen one is the crucified one.
Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.
Jesus repeats Thomas's own words back to him; though no one saw him when Thomas spoke them, he knew them. The Gospel does not say that Thomas actually touched him.
My Lord and my God!
Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.

A beatitude for every later generation, and so for us. Elisha received the spirit because he saw; we receive the Spirit believing without seeing, through the word of those who saw: “Although you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8).
ch: The Catechism quotes this evening when it teaches that the risen Christ gave his apostles his own power to forgive sins when he breathed the Holy Spirit on them (CCC 976; CCC 1485). It also notes that at the appearances of the risen Jesus the title “Lord” becomes a word of adoration, as in Thomas's confession (CCC 448). St Gregory the Great said that the unbelief of Thomas did more for our faith than the faith of the disciples who believed, because when he was led to faith by touching, our minds were released from all doubt (in substance).

qa: Was Thomas wrong to ask for proof?

He was not alone: the Gospels show that all the apostles struggled to believe, and the Catechism notes that even when faced with the risen Jesus they were still doubtful (CCC 644). Jesus does not reject Thomas. He comes back for him and meets him where he is. Yet he also says that a greater blessing belongs to those who believe without seeing, because faith rests on God's word received through the witnesses he has chosen.
Does John 20:23 have anything to do with confession to a priest?

Yes. The Church has always understood these words as the gift of the power to forgive sins in the Lord's name, given to the apostles. The Catechism teaches that since Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to his apostles, bishops, their successors, and priests, the bishops' co-workers, continue to exercise it (CCC 1461). The Council of Trent taught this explicitly. When the priest says the words of absolution, the risen Lord is still breathing peace into a closed room.
Why is this called New Sunday?

It is the Sunday that closes the white week of Easter, when in the early Church the newly baptized wore their white garments for the last time. In Kerala it is known as Puthu Njayar. The newness is the new creation that Easter has begun, and the Gospel of this day, with the Lord's breath on his disciples, shows that new creation at work.
rite: For Christians of Kerala this Sunday has a special warmth. The ancient tradition of our Churches holds that Thomas, who confessed “My Lord and my God”, brought that faith to India, and the Thomas Christians have kept it for many centuries. The Malankara Syrian Catholic Church, which prays in the West Syriac (Antiochene) tradition, belongs to this same family of St Thomas. In the Holy Qurbono, when the holy Mysteries are lifted up, many of the faithful quietly say Thomas's words, “My Lord and my God”, as an act of faith in the Lord who is present though unseen. Thomas's doubt became our blessing; his confession is our inheritance.
study: Elisha refused three times to leave his master. When has faithfulness in an ordinary, repeated way prepared me to receive something from God?
What has been handed on to me “through many witnesses”? To whom am I handing it on?
The Lord came through closed doors. What doors in my life, fear, shame or a quarrel, have I kept shut, and how might I let his “Peace be with you” in?
When I say “My Lord and my God” at the Holy Qurbono, what do I want those words to mean this year?

lead: The epistle returns to the passage from 2 Timothy read on New Sunday, and today we stay with its second half: a prisoner whose word is not chained, and a short hymn about dying and living with Christ. The Gospel is the parable of the tenants of the vineyard, which ends with a psalm verse that the first Christians loved: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Both readings speak of a rejection that God turns into victory.

r.h: The word of God is not chained
set: The writer is a prisoner treated “like a criminal” (2:9), who expects to die soon (4:6). He has just given Timothy three pictures of patient effort, the soldier, the athlete and the farmer, and now asks him to think them over. Then he points to the one memory that makes all effort worthwhile: Jesus Christ, raised from the dead.
str: v. 7: think it over; the Lord will give understanding.
vv. 8–10: remember Christ; Paul in chains; the word not chained; endurance for the sake of the elect.
vv. 11–13: the sure saying, in four lines.
kw: A formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). It marks a saying that the Church already knew and trusted, here perhaps part of an early baptismal hymn.
From deō, to bind, the same root as the “chains” (desmoi) that Paul wears. He is bound; the word is not.
The word used for Peter's denial in the Gospels (Mark 14:68, 70). The saying takes it seriously, and then shows that God's faithfulness is greater than ours.
vv: But the word of God is not chained.
Prison walls could hold the apostle but not the Gospel. While he was bound, his letters, his messengers and his example went on.
If we have died with him, we will also live with him;
Most likely a reference to Baptism, in which we die with Christ in order to rise with him (Romans 6:3–8).
if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us;
An echo of Jesus' own warning: “whoever denies me before others, I also will deny before my Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:33).
if we are faithless, he remains faithful

Here the pattern of the hymn breaks. We expect “he will be faithless too”. Instead God's faithfulness holds even when ours fails, “for he cannot deny himself”. This does not make denial harmless; verse 12 has just said the opposite. It is the ground of hope for every sinner who comes back.
ch: The Catechism teaches that through Baptism the Christian is plunged into the death of Christ and rises with him (CCC 1227), which is the first line of this hymn. The Church's martyrs, who wrote no letters, proved the second line: their chains became a pulpit, and the word went on.

r.h: The stone that the builders rejected
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem, cleansed the Temple, and been asked by the chief priests, scribes and elders by what authority he acts (11:27–33). He answers them with this parable, and verse 12 shows that it is aimed at them: “they realized that he had told this parable against them.” The parable concerns the leaders who were responsible for God's vineyard at that time, not the Jewish people as a whole; in fact the crowd protects Jesus here.

The opening words recall Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), in which the vineyard is “the house of Israel”. Every listener would have recognized it. In Isaiah the vineyard yields wild grapes; in Jesus' parable the vineyard bears fruit, but the tenants refuse to give it to the owner.
str: v. 1: the owner plants and equips the vineyard and leases it.
vv. 2–5: servant after servant is sent and mistreated.
vv. 6–8: the beloved son is sent last, killed, and thrown out.
v. 9: the owner will give the vineyard to others.
vv. 10–11: Psalm 118: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.
v. 12: the leaders understand, and want to arrest him.
kw: The same words the Father spoke at the Baptism (1:11) and the Transfiguration (9:7). In the parable Jesus speaks of himself as the last one sent, and as more than a servant.
Farm workers who rented land and paid the owner part of the harvest, a common arrangement in Jesus' day.
Literally “head of the corner”: either the great foundation stone at the corner, or the stone that crowns an arch or a wall. Either way, the most important stone in the building.
vv: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
The owner's hope seems almost foolish. That is the point: God's patience goes beyond what any human owner would show.
So they seized him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
Hebrews says that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

From Psalm 118:22, a psalm sung at the great pilgrim feasts. In Hebrew there is a play of sound between “son” (ben) and “stone” (’eben), and some commentators think it lies behind the move from parable to psalm. Peter quotes the same verse about the risen Jesus (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7).
ch: The Church reads this parable in the light of Easter: the rejected stone has been raised and made the cornerstone of a new building (CCC 756). The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ's Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living without distinction, nor against the Jews of today, and that they are not to be presented as rejected by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The parable is a warning for every steward in the Church, in every age, who might treat God's vineyard as his own.

qa: Does verse 9 mean that God has given up on Israel?

No. The parable is addressed to the leaders of that time (12:12), and the vineyard itself is not destroyed; what changes is who tends it. St Paul insists that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and the Church teaches that the Jewish people remain dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The warning is for us too: the vineyard is never ours to own.
study: “The word of God is not chained.” Where in my life does the Gospel feel bound or silenced? How might God's word still be at work there?
The tenants wanted the vineyard for themselves. What part of my life, family, work or parish, do I treat as mine rather than as God's, entrusted to me?

lead: Ephesians describes Easter happening in us: we were dead through our trespasses, and God, “rich in mercy”, made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him and seated us with him. In the Gospel Jesus rebukes a fever, and Simon's mother-in-law gets up at once and serves. Both readings have the same movement: lying down, raised up, and then service. We are saved by grace, and grace sets us to work.

r.h: By grace you have been saved
set: Ephesians is a letter of praise and teaching that bears Paul's name, addressed to Christians of Gentile background. Many scholars think it comes from a disciple who gathered Paul's thought after his death; many others hold that Paul wrote it from prison (3:1; 4:1). Chapter 1 has just praised the power God showed when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him at his right hand (1:20). Chapter 2 says that the same power has been at work in the readers.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead, following the course of this world, children of wrath.
vv. 4–7: but God: made alive with Christ, raised with him, seated with him.
vv. 8–9: saved by grace, through faith, as a gift, not as the result of works.
v. 10: God's handiwork, created for good works.
kw: One of three verbs that Ephesians forms with “together with” (syn-): made alive with, raised with, seated with (vv. 5–6). What happened to Christ at Easter is shared with those who belong to him.
God's favour, given without our deserving it. The word appears three times in this short passage (vv. 5, 7, 8).
From the verb “to make”; our word “poem” comes from it. Christians are God's handiwork, his work of art, made new in Christ.
vv: But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us
The turning point of the passage is two words: “But God”. Everything before them is human failure; everything after them is God's initiative.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
Grace is the source, and faith is the way we receive it. The whole gift, faith included, comes from God.
For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.
Works do not earn salvation, but they are its purpose. God prepared them beforehand, and by his grace we walk in them, so that the good we do is both his gift and truly ours.
ch: The Catechism teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God, the undeserved help he gives us to respond to his call (CCC 1996), and that our merit before God comes from his having chosen to associate us with the work of his grace, so that the merit of good works is to be credited first to the grace of God (CCC 2008). The Council of Trent taught that nothing that comes before justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification (Session 6, chapter 8). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation affirmed together, in their Joint Declaration, that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit of ours, we are accepted by God.

r.h: She got up and served
set: Jesus has just taught in the synagogue at Capernaum on the sabbath and delivered a man from an unclean spirit (4:31–37). Now he goes to Simon's house. Luke has not yet told the call of Simon (5:1–11), so this healing in his home comes before Simon leaves his nets. Simon was married: Paul mentions that Cephas was accompanied by a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:5).
The sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry their sick through the streets, and so the whole town comes “as the sun was setting”.
str: vv. 38–39: in Simon's house: the fever rebuked, the woman raised, her service.
v. 40: at sunset: the sick brought, hands laid on each one.
v. 41: demons driven out and silenced.
kw: Luke uses the same verb for the demon in 4:35 and for the demons in 4:41. The fever is treated like a hostile power, and Jesus speaks to it with authority.
The verb from which “deacon” comes. Her healing is complete: she takes up her place in the household and serves Jesus and the others. The tense suggests service that goes on.
Only Luke notes that Jesus laid his hands on “each of them” (v. 40). No one is healed as a face in a crowd.
vv: Then he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her.
Mark says that Jesus took her by the hand and lifted her up (Mark 1:31). Luke shows the Lord standing over the sick bed and speaking a word of command.
Immediately she got up and began to serve them.
The Greek for “got up” (anastasa) is from the same family as the word for resurrection. Read in Easter week, she is a picture of every Christian: raised up in order to serve.
and he laid his hands on each of them and cured them.
A long evening, one person at a time.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ the physician, moved by so much suffering, not only lets himself be touched by the sick but makes their miseries his own, and that he often uses signs such as the laying on of hands (CCC 1503–1504). The Church continues this care in the Anointing of the Sick, which St James describes (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510).

study: Ephesians says that God prepared good works beforehand for me to walk in. What good work is waiting for me this week?
Simon's mother-in-law got up and served at once. When God has lifted me out of an illness or a trouble, how have I used that new strength?

lead: Paul asks Gentile believers to remember where they once stood: far off, “without Christ”, “strangers to the covenants of promise”. Now, by the blood of Christ, they have been brought near, for “he is our peace”. The Gospel from Luke gives the lamp that is set on a lampstand and the warning “pay attention to how you listen”. In this week after New Sunday both readings speak of a light that has come out of the tomb: a peace that breaks down walls, and a word that must be heard well so that it can shine.

r.h: He is our peace
set: Ephesians is a letter about the Church as one body in Christ. Chapter 2 begins with what grace has done for every believer: “by grace you have been saved through faith” (2:8). Now Paul turns to his Gentile readers in particular and asks them to look back at how far they once stood from Israel's God and Israel's hope.

The letter names Paul as its author and says that he writes from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think that it was written by a disciple in Paul's name, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; in either case the Church receives it as inspired Scripture among the letters of Paul. Many commentators also think that the “dividing wall” would remind a reader of that time of the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple beyond which Gentiles could not go. A stone inscription from it, found in 1871, warns them not to pass.
str: vv. 11–12: remember: once you were far off, without Christ, strangers to the covenants, without hope.
v. 13: but now in Christ Jesus you have been brought near by his blood.
vv. 14–16: he is our peace; he has made the two into one new humanity and reconciled both to God through the cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to the far and the near; through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
¶ Verse 18 names the Father, the Son and the Spirit in one sentence: through Christ, in the Spirit, to the Father. This is the shape of all Christian prayer.
kw: In the Bible peace (Hebrew shalom) is more than the end of a quarrel. It is wholeness, things set right between God and people and among people. Here peace is a person: “he is our peace”.
A word found only here in the New Testament. The letter explains it at once: the wall is “the hostility between us”.
The word for being brought into the presence of a king. It appears also in Romans 5:2. Through Christ the Gentile, once a stranger, may now come straight to the Father.
vv: remember that you were at that time without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise

Notice what the Gentiles lacked: the Christ whom Israel awaited, Israel's covenants and Israel's hope. The covenants with Israel are the treasure, and to be outside them was the loss. The Church does not take Israel's place: the Gentiles are brought near to promises that remain Israel's, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
“Far” and “near” come from Isaiah 57:19, which verse 17 will quote. Nearness is not earned; it is given by the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Christ does not only bring peace; he is peace. In his own flesh, offered on the Cross, the enmity is ended.
He has abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances,

This must be read with care. The letter does not throw away God's moral law, which it quotes in 6:2. What is set aside is the law as a fence that kept the peoples apart, with its rules of separation. In Christ, Jew and Gentile meet in one new humanity.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
“Both of us”: the Jew who was near and the Gentile who was far now come to the Father by the same door.
ch: The Second Vatican Council recalls this passage when it speaks of the Jewish people: the Church believes that by his cross Christ our Peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism teaches that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ, who by the blood of his Cross put the hostility to death (CCC 2305). So the first fruit of Easter is a reconciled people. Every Holy Qurbono, where people of every family, language and background receive the one Body, shows the wall already broken.

r.h: Pay attention to how you listen
set: Jesus has told the parable of the sower and explained it: the seed is the word of God, and the good soil is those who “hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance” (8:15). These three sayings follow at once. Just after them, Jesus says that his true family are “those who hear the word of God and do it” (8:21). So the whole passage is about hearing.
Luke gives the lamp saying a second time in 11:33, and Mark places the same group of sayings after the sower (Mark 4:21–25).
str: v. 16: no one hides a lit lamp; it is put on a lampstand so that those who come in may see.
v. 17: what is hidden will be made known.
v. 18: so take care how you listen: more will be given to the one who has.
kw: A small clay oil lamp, lit in the evening and set high so that the whole room had light. In Luke the lamp is the word received and lived, which cannot be kept private.
Mark has “what you hear” (Mark 4:24); Luke writes “how”. The question is not only which words reach us, but with what heart we take them in.
Luke adds the word “seem”, which Mark does not have. A faith that is only heard and never kept was never truly ours.
vv: No one after lighting a lamp hides it under a jar, or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light.
Luke speaks of “those who enter”, people coming into the house. The light is for guests. In Acts the same Luke will show the light of Easter going out to people of every nation.
For nothing is hidden that will not be disclosed, nor is anything secret that will not become known and come to light.

On the lips of Jesus this is first a promise: the mystery of the Kingdom, still veiled in parables, will be made known. After the Resurrection the apostles proclaim openly what they once heard in private.
Then pay attention to how you listen;
“Then” ties the warning to what came before. Because the word is meant to shine, the hearer carries a responsibility.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its teaching on revelation with the words “Hearing the word of God with reverence” (Dei Verbum 1), and it asks all the faithful to come often to the Scriptures in reading and prayer (Dei Verbum 25). The Catechism adds that prayer should accompany the reading of Sacred Scripture, so that a dialogue takes place between God and man (CCC 2653). Luke himself shows the Mother of the Lord as the first of those who hear well: she treasured all these things in her heart (Luke 2:19, 51).

qa: Does “to those who have, more will be given” mean that God favours the rich?

No. Jesus is not speaking of money but of the word. The one who “has” is the one who receives the word and keeps it, and such a person grows in understanding. The one who does not open the heart loses even the little that seemed to be there. It is a law of the spiritual life, and a call to listen now.
study: Who first set the light of faith where I could see it? How can I do the same for someone who comes into my home?
In my family or parish, where does a “dividing wall” still stand? What would it mean to let Christ, our peace, break it down this week?

lead: Today the Panchangam remembers Most Rev. Lawrence Mar Ephrem, a bishop of our Church and the first Bishop of Marthandom, who died in 1997, and the readings fit a day of remembering shepherds. Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith, because “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever”, and it speaks of an altar and a sacrifice of praise. In Matthew, Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise servant whom the master will find at work when he comes. The Panchangam also allows John 10:11–18, the Good Shepherd who lays down his life and takes it up again, the risen Lord in whom both readings meet.

r.h: Remember your leaders
set: Hebrews is a long sermon on the priesthood of Christ, sent as a letter to Christians who were weary and tempted to fall back (10:32–36; 12:12). It does not name its author. From early times many in the East linked it with Paul, and the Church long counted it among his letters, while most scholars today think that it was written by another teacher of the first generation. Chapter 13 gathers last counsels: love of the brothers and sisters, hospitality, faithfulness in marriage, and trust in God rather than in money (13:1–6).

Verse 7 speaks of leaders who “spoke the word of God”, and asks the readers to consider “the outcome of their way of life”. Many commentators think that these were the founders of the community who had already died, perhaps as witnesses for Christ. Later, in 13:17, the letter speaks of the leaders now living.
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ is the same for ever.
v. 9: do not be carried away by strange teachings; the heart is strengthened by grace.
vv. 10–12: we have an altar; as the sin offering was burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate.
vv. 13–14: let us go to him outside the camp, for we seek the city that is to come.
vv. 15–16: offer a sacrifice of praise, and do not neglect to do good and to share.
kw: Literally “those who lead”. The letter uses the word three times in this chapter (13:7, 17, 24). Their authority is bound to the word of God that they spoke.

The ordinary word for an altar of sacrifice. Many Catholic commentators hear in “we have an altar” the table of the Lord's Body and Blood; others think first of the Cross itself. The two belong together, for the altar makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross.
An Old Testament phrase for a thanksgiving offering. The letter explains it as “the fruit of lips that confess his name”, an echo of Hosea 14:2 in its Greek form.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Three verbs: remember, consider, imitate. To remember a bishop rightly is to look at how his life ended and to copy his faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders die; the Lord they preached does not change. That is why their faith can be imitated: it rested on the same Christ who is with us today.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.

On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Jesus died outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:20), and the letter sees in this the fulfilment of that rite.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
The praise of this verse and the sharing of verse 16 do not replace the one sacrifice of Christ: they flow from it. We receive at the altar, and our life becomes an offering.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is the sacrifice of praise by which the Church sings the glory of God in the name of all creation (CCC 1361), and that in it the lives of the faithful, their praise, sufferings, prayer and work, are united with the offering of Christ (CCC 1368). So it is fitting to remember a departed bishop at the Holy Qurbono: we pray for him at the same altar from which he fed us.

r.h: The servant found at work
set: Jesus is speaking on the Mount of Olives about the end of the age and his coming (24:3). He has just said, “Keep awake therefore, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming” (24:42). Now he gives the first of several parables about waiting: the servant left in charge, the ten bridesmaids and the talents (25:1–30).

Luke has the same parable (Luke 12:42–46), where it answers Peter's question whether it is meant for the disciples or for everyone (12:41). In both Gospels it speaks most directly to those whom the master has put “in charge of his household”.
str: v. 45: who is the faithful and wise servant set over the household?
vv. 46–47: blessed is the one found at work; he will be set over all.
vv. 48–49: the wicked servant thinks, “My master is delayed”, and abuses the others.
vv. 50–51: the master comes at an unexpected hour, and the end is weeping.
kw: The NRSV says “slave”. In the households of that time a trusted slave could manage the whole estate. Christian leaders are servants of the household, not its owners.
Practical good sense, the wisdom of one who sees what the hour requires. The wise bridesmaids in 25:2 are given the same word.
The master takes his time. The danger is not the delay itself but what the servant does with it.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The task is simple and daily: food at the right time. The Church has always heard in it the duty of pastors to give the word and the sacraments faithfully.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The blessing is not for one who guesses the date but for one who is found doing the work.
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’
Evil begins with a sentence spoken inside: there is time. The beating of fellow servants and the drinking follow from forgetting that the master will come.
ch: The Catechism says that the time between the Lord's Ascension and his coming in glory is a time of waiting and watching (CCC 672). St Augustine, speaking of his own office, told his people that for them he was a bishop and with them he was a Christian, and that the first name was a danger while the second was salvation (Sermon 340, in substance). This parable keeps that danger and that hope before every shepherd.

qa: What does “he will cut him in pieces” mean?

The words are strong on purpose, in the style of a prophetic warning. Many scholars think that the phrase means to cut off, to separate the servant from the household, which fits the next words, “put him with the hypocrites”. The point is that a servant who abuses the trust given to him cannot remain in the master's house. Jesus warns in order to save, and the Church prays that none of her shepherds may come to such an end.
rite: Most Rev. Lawrence Mar Ephrem, whom the Panchangam remembers today, was a bishop of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, the first Bishop of Marthandom, who died in 1997. Our Antiochene tradition remembers its departed fathers and shepherds in the intercessions of every Holy Qurbono. To remember him with Hebrews 13 is to thank God for the word he spoke, to look at the faith in which he died, and to pray that the Lord give him rest.
study: Who first spoke the word of God to me? How can I thank God for that person today, and imitate that faith?
If the Master came today, what work would he find me doing for his household?

lead: Paul tells his own story: the zealous persecutor whom God had set apart before he was born and called by grace, and to whom God was pleased “to reveal his Son”. The churches of Judea heard of it, “and they glorified God because of me.” The Gospel shows the disciples arguing about who is the greatest, and Jesus setting a little child beside him. Both readings show what the risen Lord does with human greatness: Paul's zeal is turned into a mission, and the disciples' ambition is turned toward the least.

r.h: God was pleased to reveal his Son to me
set: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, in the interior of what is now Turkey, because teachers had come after him saying that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the whole Law of Moses. They seem also to have said that Paul's gospel was second-hand, learned from others. So Paul tells how he received it: “I did not receive it from a human source” (1:12).

Paul never stopped being a Jew (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5). What changed was that God showed him Jesus as his Son. Many scholars therefore prefer to call what happened to him a call, like the call of the prophets, rather than a change of religion. His own words echo Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1.
str: vv. 13–14: my earlier life: persecutor of the church, zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.
vv. 15–16a: but God set me apart, called me, and revealed his Son to me for the Gentiles.
vv. 16b–17: I consulted no one; I went to Arabia and returned to Damascus.
vv. 18–20: after three years, fifteen days with Cephas; of the other apostles I saw only James.
vv. 21–24: in Syria and Cilicia; the churches of Judea glorified God.
kw: In the New Testament the word appears only here (1:13, 14). It means the Jewish way of life, lived with zeal. Paul is not mocking it; he is saying how far he had advanced in it.
God set Paul apart “before I was born”, literally from his mother's womb, as with Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5). The call was older than the persecution.
The word means to visit in order to get to know someone and to learn. Paul went up to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas, that is, Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days.
vv: I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it.
Paul does not soften his past. He calls the community he persecuted “the church of God”, the gathering that belongs to God.
But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased
Every word puts the first move with God: he set apart, he called, he was pleased. Grace comes before any merit of Paul's.
Then after three years I did go up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and stayed with him fifteen days;
Paul insists that his gospel came from the Lord, yet he goes to Peter. The gospel he received by revelation is the same gospel that the apostles in Jerusalem keep.
And they glorified God because of me.
The last word of the story is praise. A changed life gives glory to God, not to the one who was changed.
ch: The Catechism quotes verses 15 and 16 when it explains the title Son of God: at the moment of his conversion on the road to Damascus, Paul came to know Jesus as the Son, as Peter had confessed him (CCC 442). Paul's life became the Church's great sign that no one is beyond the reach of grace, and that the persecutor can become the apostle.

r.h: The least among you is the greatest
set: This scene comes at the end of Jesus' ministry in Galilee. He has just told the disciples for the second time that he will be handed over, and Luke says that they did not understand and were afraid to ask (9:44–45). Into that silence comes an argument about rank. Soon afterwards Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51).
In the world of that time a small child had no standing, no rights of its own and nothing to offer. To welcome a child was to welcome someone who could give nothing back.
str: v. 46: the argument: who is the greatest?
v. 47: Jesus knows their thoughts and sets a child beside him.
v. 48: to welcome the child is to welcome Jesus and the Father; the least is the greatest.
kw: The same word names the argument among them in verse 46 and the “inner thoughts” that Jesus reads in verse 47. Rivalry in the heart becomes rivalry in speech.
A small child. Jesus does not only speak about the child; he puts it “by his side”, the place of honour next to himself.
Literally “the smaller”. Jesus turns the scale around: in his Kingdom greatness is measured by smallness.
vv: An argument arose among them as to which one of them was the greatest.
Luke places this right after Jesus spoke of his Passion. The disciples were thinking of places of honour while he was thinking of the Cross.
But Jesus, aware of their inner thoughts, took a little child and put it by his side,
Jesus answers a hidden thought with an action before a word. The child standing beside him is the answer.
Whoever welcomes this child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me;
A chain of welcome: the child, Jesus, the Father. Whoever receives the smallest person receives God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the Kingdom, and that for this we must humble ourselves and become little (CCC 526). Paul's own story fits this Gospel: the man who had advanced beyond many of his own age later called himself “the least of the apostles” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

qa: Paul calls James “the Lord's brother”. Did Jesus have brothers?

In the language of the Bible “brother” can mean a close relative. The Hebrew of Genesis calls Lot, Abraham's nephew, his “brother” (Genesis 14:14, 16). The Church has always professed that the Mother of the Lord remained ever virgin, and the Catechism explains that the “brothers” of Jesus are close relations of his (CCC 500). St Jerome argued this at length from Scripture (in substance). James, a leader of the church in Jerusalem, was such a kinsman of the Lord.
study: Paul's zeal for God was real, but misdirected until God showed him his Son. Where might my zeal need to be turned by Christ?
Who is the “little child” in my world today, someone who can give me nothing back? How will I welcome that person in Christ's name?

lead: After fourteen years Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, and lays his gospel before the leaders, “so that the truth of the gospel might always remain with you.” In Luke, Jesus mourns over the lakeside towns that saw his mighty works and did not repent, and then gives his messengers a great dignity: “Whoever listens to you listens to me.” Both readings show the gospel carried by people who are sent, and who remain in communion with the Lord who sends them.

r.h: That the truth of the gospel might remain
set: Paul continues his account. After his first short visit to Peter (1:18), fourteen years pass. Now he goes up again, and this time the question is the one troubling the Galatians: must Gentile believers be circumcised?

Scholars discuss how this visit fits the story in Acts. Many identify it with the meeting at Jerusalem in Acts 15, where the apostles and elders decided that Gentiles were not to be burdened with circumcision; others link it with the earlier visit to bring help in a time of famine (Acts 11:29–30). Either way, Paul's point is that the leaders in Jerusalem recognized his gospel.
str: vv. 1–2: after fourteen years, with Barnabas and Titus, Paul goes up in response to a revelation and lays his gospel before the leaders.
v. 3: Titus, a Greek, is not compelled to be circumcised.
vv. 4–5: false believers try to bring them into bondage; Paul does not give way.
v. 6: the leaders add nothing to his gospel; God shows no partiality.
kw: Literally “those who are reckoned”, those of repute. In verse 9 Paul names them: James, Cephas and John.
Not a formula but the gospel's real content: that in Christ the Gentiles are received by grace through faith, without first having to become Jews.
Literally “receives a face”, a Hebrew way of speaking for judging by appearance or rank. God does not.
vv: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.
Barnabas was a Jewish believer from Cyprus (Acts 4:36); Titus was a Greek. The two companions are the question in person.

Then I laid before them (though only in a private meeting with the acknowledged leaders) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain.
Paul, who received his gospel by revelation, still seeks communion with the apostles. He knows that a gospel cut off from the Church would be running in vain.
we did not submit to them even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might always remain with you.

The “false believers” of verse 4 were members of the Church who insisted on circumcision; Paul's quarrel is with them, not with the Jewish people. His firmness is for the sake of others: “with you”. He defends the Galatians' place in the family of God.
ch: The Church has always seen in this meeting, together with Acts 15, a pattern for settling questions of faith: the apostles meet, listen and decide together under the Holy Spirit. The Catechism teaches that the college of bishops, united with the successor of Peter, carries on this care for the whole Church (CCC 880–883). Paul's words also stand behind the Church's teaching that our justification comes from the grace of God (CCC 1996), a grace that bears fruit in “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

r.h: Whoever listens to you listens to me
set: Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem and has sent out seventy messengers ahead of him (10:1). He has told them what to do when a town does not receive them (10:10–12). Now he turns to the towns beside the Sea of Galilee, where so many of his mighty works had been done.

Chorazin lay in the hills a few kilometres north of Capernaum. Bethsaida, the town of Andrew, Peter and Philip (John 1:44), lay near the place where the Jordan enters the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast, often rebuked by the prophets (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28).
str: vv. 13–14: woe to Chorazin and Bethsaida; Tyre and Sidon would have repented.
v. 15: Capernaum will be brought down to Hades.
v. 16: whoever listens to you listens to me; whoever rejects you rejects me and the one who sent me.
kw: A cry of grief as much as of warning, the word of a lament. Jesus mourns over these towns as he warns them.
Literally “powers”, the word the first three Gospels use for the miracles. They were signs calling for a change of heart.
To change one's mind and turn one's life around. Sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of such turning (Jonah 3:6).
vv: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!
Chorazin is named only here and in Matthew's parallel (Matthew 11:21), and no miracle there is recorded. We learn from this verse how much Jesus did that is not written (John 21:25).
And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.
The words recall Isaiah 14:13–15, the taunt against the proud king of Babylon. Capernaum, the town Jesus made his home, is warned not to be proud of its privilege.
Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.
A chain of sending, from the Father to Jesus to his messengers. The Easter Church lives by it: the risen Lord still speaks through those he sends.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes verse 16 when it teaches that the bishops have succeeded the apostles as shepherds of the Church, so that whoever hears them hears Christ (Lumen Gentium 20). The Catechism recalls the same words when it explains why the faithful receive the teaching of their pastors with docility (CCC 87). This is not a claim to human greatness: the messengers carry a word that is not their own.

qa: Why did Paul refuse to have Titus circumcised, when Acts says that he had Timothy circumcised (Acts 16:3)?

The two cases were different. Titus was a Greek, and some were demanding his circumcision as necessary for salvation; to give way would have denied that we are saved by the grace of Christ. Timothy had a Jewish mother, and Paul had him circumcised by his own choice, so that he could work among Jews without giving offence (Acts 16:1–3). Paul was firm on the principle and flexible in love (1 Corinthians 9:20).
study: Paul defended “the truth of the gospel” with firmness and in communion with the apostles. Where do I need both courage and communion in my faith?
Jesus says, “Whoever listens to you listens to me.” How do I listen to the pastors and teachers of the Church in my life?

lead: On this Second Sunday after Qyomtho the Church's table is again rich. The Evening Gospel (John 21:15–19) gives the Lord's threefold question to Peter, “Do you love me?”, and his command, “Feed my sheep.” Four Old Testament lessons follow: the song of Moses at the sea (Exodus 15:1–8); the word of Wisdom that “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:12–16); the priests with their trumpets going round the walls of Jericho (Joshua 6:8–14); and the one who comes from Edom, “mighty to save” (Isaiah 63:1–6). In Acts 13:26–41 Paul preaches at Antioch in Pisidia that God raised Jesus, and that “he whom God raised up experienced no corruption.”

We study three of these closely. Exodus is the lesson nearest to the Gospel: both take place at the sea, and in both the Lord saves as night turns to morning (Exodus 14:24, 27). Ephesians closes with a call to pray at all times and a blessing of peace, love and grace. John shows the risen Lord on the shore at daybreak, the great catch, and the breakfast he has prepared. The line runs from the sea that covered the enemy to the sea that gives up a net full of fish, and its key words are sea, daybreak and It is the Lord!

r.h: I will sing to the Lord
set: Israel has just crossed the sea on dry ground, and the Egyptian chariots that followed them have been covered by the returning waters (14:21–31). Chapter 14 ends, “So the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses” (14:31). Their first answer to salvation is a song.

The Song of the Sea is counted among the oldest poems in the Bible, and many scholars think that its language is older than the prose around it. Miriam takes up its opening words with the women and their tambourines (15:20–21). The reading gives the first part of the song, which tells of the victory at the sea; the second part tells of God leading his people to his holy dwelling (15:13–18).
str: v. 1: Moses and Israel sing: horse and rider thrown into the sea.
vv. 2–3: the Lord is my strength, my salvation, my God; the Lord is a warrior.
vv. 4–5: Pharaoh's chariots sink like a stone.
vv. 6–7: your right hand, O Lord, shatters the enemy.
v. 8: at the blast of your nostrils the waters stood up in a heap.
¶ The song moves from telling the story (vv. 1–5) to speaking to God directly (vv. 6–8). Israel first says what happened, and then turns to the one who did it.
kw: “He has become my salvation” (v. 2). The word means rescue, deliverance, victory. The name Jesus (Yeshua) comes from the same root and means “the Lord saves” (CCC 430).
Literally “a man of war” (v. 3). Israel did not fight at the sea; the Lord fought for them, as Moses had said: “The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still” (14:14).

“At the blast of your nostrils” (v. 8). The same Hebrew word means wind, breath and spirit. The strong east wind of 14:21 is here the very breath of God, like the wind from God that swept over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2).
vv: I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
These are also the words of Miriam's refrain (15:21). The first great song in the Bible is a song of thanksgiving for salvation.
The Lord is my strength and my might, and he has become my salvation;

A note on the text. The Hebrew word rendered “might” (zimrāt) can also mean “song”, and many translations read “my strength and my song”. Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14 repeat this line, and it became one of Israel's great confessions of faith.
The Lord is a warrior; the Lord is his name.
The battle belongs to God, not to Israel. The name of the Lord, made known to Moses at the bush (3:14–15), is now known by what he has done.
At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up, the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
The poem paints the sea as a wall that stands still at God's breath. The deep, which the old stories of the nations pictured as a power fighting the gods, obeys the Lord without a struggle.
ch: The Church has always read the crossing of the sea as a figure of Baptism. Paul says that our ancestors “were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2), and the Catechism teaches that the crossing of the Red Sea, the liberation of Israel from slavery in Egypt, announces the liberation brought about by Baptism (CCC 1221). The Book of Revelation shows those who have conquered standing beside a sea of glass and singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3). So the song of Exodus becomes the Church's own Easter song: the Lord has passed through death, and his people come up out of the water singing.

r.h: Pray in the Spirit at all times
set: Ephesians ends its teaching on Christian life with the armour of God (6:10–17): truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”. Our reading follows straight on. Prayer is not one more piece of armour; it is the way all of it is worn.

The letter presents Paul as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). Many scholars think that Ephesians was written in Paul's name by a disciple, while others hold that Paul wrote it himself; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture among the letters of Paul. Verses 21–22 are almost word for word the same as Colossians 4:7–8, and in both letters Tychicus is the messenger.
str: v. 18: pray in the Spirit at all times; keep alert; persevere in prayer for all the saints.
vv. 19–20: pray for me, an ambassador in chains, that I may speak boldly.
vv. 21–22: Tychicus will bring news and encourage you.
vv. 23–24: peace, love with faith, and grace to all who love the Lord.
kw: Kairos is time as occasion, the moment at hand. The call is to pray in every situation, whatever the hour brings.
Open, confident speech, the speech of one who has nothing to hide. In Acts it is the mark of the apostles after Easter (Acts 4:13, 31). Paul asks for it as a gift of prayer, not as a natural talent.
An ambassador was protected by his office; this one is in chains. The paradox is the gospel's own: the King's envoy is a prisoner, and yet “the word of God is not chained” (2 Timothy 2:9).
