vv: Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication.
Prayer “in the Spirit” is prayer that the Spirit stirs and carries (Romans 8:26). It is not limited to set hours, though set hours teach us how to pray at all times.
keep alert and always persevere in supplication for all the saints.
“The saints” are all the baptized. Christians pray not only for themselves but for the whole Church.
Pray also for me, so that when I speak, a message may be given to me to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel,
The apostle asks the people to pray for him. The shepherd needs the prayers of the flock.
Grace be with all who have an undying love for our Lord Jesus Christ.

A note on the text. The last Greek words are literally “in incorruption”. The NRSV joins them to love, “an undying love”; the Malayalam POC joins them to the gift, “grace and eternal life”. Both readings are possible, and both are true: love for the risen Lord shares in his life that does not decay.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 18 in its teaching on praying constantly, and explains that this is not a matter of many words but of a heart turned toward God at all times (CCC 2742–2745). It also shows that the first Christian communities lived the prayer of intercession intensely, and that the apostle both prayed for them and asked their prayer for his preaching (CCC 2636). Our Antiochene tradition lives this rhythm in its seven times of prayer, which begin in the evening and run through the night and day, so that the whole day is offered.

r.h: It is the Lord!
set: John's Gospel seems to end at 20:30–31, with the words “these are written so that you may come to believe”. Chapter 21 follows as an epilogue. Many scholars think that it was added by the evangelist or by his disciples, who speak in 21:24 (“we know that his testimony is true”). No ancient manuscript of the Gospel lacks it, and the Church receives it as part of the inspired Gospel.

The scene moves from Jerusalem back to Galilee, to the Sea of Tiberias, John's name for the Sea of Galilee (6:1). Seven disciples are there, Peter first and Thomas second, and they have gone back to the work they knew. Earlier in the Gospel Peter denied the Lord beside a charcoal fire (18:18); here he will meet him beside another.
str: vv. 1–3: seven disciples; Peter goes fishing; that night they catch nothing.
vv. 4–6: at daybreak Jesus stands on the beach: “Cast the net to the right side”; the net is full.
vv. 7–8: the beloved disciple says, “It is the Lord!”; Peter jumps into the sea.
vv. 9–11: a charcoal fire, fish and bread; Peter hauls ashore a hundred and fifty-three large fish, and the net is not torn.
vv. 12–14: “Come and have breakfast”; Jesus gives them bread and fish; the third appearance.
kw: The passage begins and ends with this verb (21:1, 14). It is John's word for Jesus making his glory known, as at Cana (2:11). The risen Lord is not found by searching; he shows himself.
The word a father uses for his little ones, or an older man for younger friends. The first word of the risen Lord to tired fishermen is tender.

This word appears only twice in the New Testament: here, and at the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter denied Jesus (18:18). The Lord himself lights the fire beside which Peter will be healed.
vv: They went out and got into the boat, but that night they caught nothing.
In John night is more than a time of day (3:2; 13:30). Without the Lord the work of the night is empty.
Just after daybreak, Jesus stood on the beach; but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.

As with Mary Magdalene at the tomb (20:14) and the two on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:16), the risen Lord is not recognized at once. He is the same, yet he is known only when he gives himself to be known.
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
Love sees first; Peter acts first. The beloved disciple recognizes him, and Peter throws himself into the sea to reach him. The Church needs both.
full of large fish, a hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.

The Greek verb for “torn” is the one from which our word “schism” comes. It is the same verb the soldiers used of Jesus' seamless tunic: “Let us not tear it” (19:24). The net that holds so many and does not break is a picture of the one Church.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.
These are the same actions as at the feeding of the five thousand beside this same sea (6:11). The risen Lord feeds his own with his own hands.
ch: The Catechism explains that the risen Jesus showed his disciples that he was not a ghost by inviting them to touch him and by sharing their meal, and it cites this chapter (CCC 645). St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, saw in the hundred and fifty-three fish all who are saved by grace: 153 is the sum of all the numbers from 1 to 17, and 17 joins the 10 of the Law to the 7 of the Spirit (Tractates on John 122, in substance). St Jerome reports that the naturalists of his day counted a hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish, so that the catch stands for every people (Commentary on Ezekiel, on 47:9–12, in substance). The Fathers differ in the detail but agree on the meaning: the Church's net is for all, and it holds.

qa: Why did the disciples not recognize Jesus at first?

The Gospels describe the same thing more than once (John 20:14; Luke 24:16). The risen body of Jesus is truly his own body, which bears the wounds, but it now has the new properties of a glorious body: it is not limited by space and time, and he appears how and when he wills (CCC 645). Recognition comes as a gift, through a word, a sign or a shared meal. That is still how we recognize him.
Is the number 153 meant to be a code?

John gives the number as a fact, the kind of thing fishermen count, and it suggests the memory of an eyewitness. The Fathers were also sure that it carries a meaning, and they offered several explanations; none of them is certain. What John himself underlines is that the net, though so full, was not torn. The fullness and the unity of the Church are the point.
The song of Moses calls the Lord a warrior and rejoices that Pharaoh's army was drowned. How should Christians pray it?

The song celebrates God's rescue of a people of slaves from a power that would not let them go. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the books of the Old Testament contain “some things which are incomplete and temporary” (Dei Verbum 15) and are to be read in the light of Christ. In Christ the true enemy is revealed: sin and death, which he overthrew by his own death and Resurrection. This is why the Fathers read this song as a song of Baptism. It is not a song against any people.
rite: On this Second Sunday after Qyomtho the Evening Gospel already gives the scene that follows today's breakfast: Peter, who denied the Lord three times, is asked three times, “Do you love me?”, and is told, “Feed my sheep.” The Catechism sees in these words the risen Lord confirming the charge he had given to Peter (CCC 553). For the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church these words have a special warmth: in 1930 Mar Ivanios and those who came with him entered full communion with the successor of Peter, while keeping the whole Antiochene heritage. The breakfast on the shore is also an image of every Holy Qurbono: the risen Lord prepares the table, takes the bread and gives it to his own.
study: The disciples worked all night and caught nothing. Where am I working hard without listening for the Lord's word from the shore?
Moses and Israel answered their rescue with a song. What has the Lord done for me this season of Qyomtho that deserves my thanks aloud?
Ephesians asks us to pray “for all the saints”. For whom in the Church, near or far, will I pray by name this week?
Who in my parish or family is like the beloved disciple, quick to say, “It is the Lord!”? How can I learn to recognize him in the ordinary work of my day?

lead: Today the Church remembers St Julius, Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. St Paul tells us what the Easter peace is: “since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and even suffering becomes a road to a hope that does not disappoint. In Matthew, Jesus says that whoever welcomes his messengers welcomes him, and that not even a cup of cold water given to a little one will be forgotten. St Julius lived both readings: he stood firm in the faith of Nicaea and welcomed St Athanasius when he was driven from his see.

r.h: We have peace with God
set: In Romans 1–4 Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need the grace of God, and that God makes people righteous through faith in Christ, as he reckoned Abraham righteous through faith (4:3). Chapter 4 ends with an Easter confession: Jesus “was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification” (4:25). Chapter 5 begins with what follows from this.
str: vv. 1–2: justified by faith, we have peace with God, access to grace and the hope of glory.
vv. 3–4: we boast even in sufferings: suffering, endurance, character, hope.
v. 5: hope does not disappoint, for God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
kw: Made righteous, set right with God. In the Catholic faith this is not only a verdict: God forgives sin and truly renews the person within (CCC 1989).
Literally the quality of something that has been tested and proved, like metal that has passed through the fire.
The tense tells of something done that goes on: the love was poured and is still flowing. The image recalls God's promise, “I will pour out my spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28).
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

A note on the text. Many ancient manuscripts read “let us have peace” instead of “we have peace”; in Greek the two differ by a single letter. Most editors prefer “we have”, as the NRSV does, while the Malayalam POC follows the other reading. Both are true: peace is a gift given, and a gift to be lived.
through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand;
Grace is not a passing visit but ground to stand on.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
Hope does not put us to shame, for it rests not on our own strength but on God's love already given. “God's love” here is first God's love for us, and it becomes our love for him.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 5 when it teaches that God is Love and that love is his first gift, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (CCC 733). It calls justification the most excellent work of God's love (CCC 1994). St Augustine returned to this verse again and again, above all in his work On the Spirit and the Letter, where it is the key to his teaching that grace is the love of God given to us (in substance).

r.h: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me
set: These verses close the missionary discourse of Matthew 10, in which Jesus sends the Twelve to proclaim that the Kingdom of heaven has come near (10:7). He has warned them of rejection and persecution (10:16–39). He ends with the other side: the welcome they will receive, and its reward.

Jewish teaching of the time knew the principle that a person's envoy is like the person himself (Mishnah, Berakhot 5:5). Jesus takes it further: the one who receives his messenger receives him, and through him the Father.
str: v. 40: to welcome you is to welcome me and the one who sent me.
v. 41: to welcome a prophet or a righteous person brings their reward.
v. 42: even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones will not lose its reward.
kw: To receive a guest into one's house. For travelling missionaries, welcome meant a roof, a meal and a hearing.
In Matthew these are the disciples themselves, ordinary believers without rank (18:6, 10, 14). The least disciple carries the Lord's honour.
The smallest gift a poor home could offer. In a hot land, cool water from a deep well was itself a kindness.
vv: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
Hospitality becomes a meeting with God. The door opened to the messenger is opened to the Father.
and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple
“In the name of a disciple” means because he is a disciple, for Christ's sake. The gift is small, but the reason gives it weight.
truly I tell you, none of these will lose their reward.
The reward is not a wage earned but the generosity of God, who notices what everyone else forgets.
ch: The Catechism teaches that our merit before God comes from his grace, which goes before us and goes with us, so that every reward is first his gift (CCC 2008–2011). St Julius is a living commentary on verse 40. When St Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, was driven from his see for holding to the faith of Nicaea, Julius received him at Rome, and a council held there under Julius declared him innocent. In welcoming the persecuted bishop, the Bishop of Rome welcomed Christ.

qa: Paul says that we are justified by faith. Does that make good works unimportant?

No. The Catholic Church teaches that we are justified by grace, received through faith and Baptism, and that this grace makes us truly righteous and bears fruit in works of love. Good works done in grace are pleasing to God and merit reward, but only because God's grace first made them possible (CCC 2008, 2010). Today's Gospel shows it: even a cup of cold water given for Christ's sake is not forgotten.
rite: St Julius I was Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352, in the years of the great struggle over the faith of Nicaea. His letter to the bishops gathered at Antioch, which St Athanasius preserved, pleads for fairness and for the communion of the Churches. The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, Antiochene in heritage and in full communion with the successor of Peter, can see in him a Pope who cared for the faith and the bishops of the East.
study: Paul says that suffering can produce endurance, character and hope. What present difficulty can I offer to God so that it becomes a road to hope?
Whom can I welcome this week in Christ's name, even with a small kindness like a cup of cold water?

lead: Both readings today are about prayer, and both go back to the source. Hebrews shows the Son himself praying “with loud cries and tears” and being heard, so that he became our High Priest. Luke shows the disciples watching Jesus pray and asking him to teach them, and he gives them the Our Father. The prayer of the Son becomes the prayer of his brothers and sisters. The key words are heard, priest and Father.

r.h: He was heard because of his reverent submission
set: The Letter to the Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It reads like a long sermon to Christians who were growing tired and tempted to drift away. The writer does not give his name. Our Syriac tradition, with much of the ancient Church, counted it among the letters of St Paul, and many scholars today think it came from someone in his circle. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.

In 5:1–4 the writer has described what any high priest must be: taken from among people, gentle with the ignorant, and called by God, not self-appointed. Today's verses show how Christ fulfils each point.
str: vv. 5–6: Christ did not appoint himself: two psalms show the Father's call (Psalm 2:7; Psalm 110:4).
vv. 7–8: his prayer and his obedience in suffering.
vv. 9–10: made perfect, he becomes the source of salvation and is named High Priest.
kw: Reverence before God, the awe of one who trusts and yields. The Son was heard not because he escaped death but because he handed himself over to the Father with complete trust.

In Hebrews this does not mean that Christ was once morally imperfect. It means brought to the goal, completed. The same family of words was used for the consecration of priests. Through his Passion and Resurrection the Son reaches the fullness of his work as Priest.

The king of Salem and “priest of God Most High” who brought out bread and wine to Abraham (Genesis 14:18). Psalm 110:4 names a priesthood “according to the order of Melchizedek”, and Hebrews applies it to Christ.
vv: So also Christ did not glorify himself in becoming a high priest,
Every true priesthood is received, not taken. This is true of the Son, and it is true of those who share his priesthood in the Church.
Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death,
The words recall Gethsemane, where Jesus prayed, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (Luke 22:42). Hebrews does not hide the human anguish of the Son.
and he was heard because of his reverent submission.
He was not spared the Cross. He was heard in a deeper way: the Father brought him through death and raised him. In this Easter season we read the verse in the light of the empty tomb.
he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,
He learned obedience by suffering, and those who obey him receive salvation from him. The obedience of the Head becomes the way of the members.
ch: The Catechism sees in the agony of Gethsemane the Son's acceptance of the cup from the Father (CCC 612), and it teaches that the Father answered the cry of his Son beyond all hope by raising him from the dead (CCC 2606). It also says that the Christian tradition sees Melchizedek as a figure of the priesthood of Christ (CCC 1544). St Cyprian already joined the bread and wine of Melchizedek to the Eucharist (Letter 63, in substance). Every Holy Qurbono is offered through this one High Priest.

r.h: Lord, teach us to pray
set: Luke more than any other evangelist shows Jesus at prayer: at his baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before asking “Who do you say that I am?” (9:18), and at the Transfiguration (9:28–29). Here the disciples watch him pray and want to learn. John the Baptist had taught his disciples a way of prayer, and they ask for one of their own.
Luke's form of the Lord's Prayer is shorter than Matthew's (Matthew 6:9–13). The prayer the Church uses in the liturgy follows Matthew.
str: v. 1: Jesus at prayer; the request.
v. 2: the address and two petitions for God's name and kingdom.
vv. 3–4: three petitions for our needs: bread, forgiveness, protection in trial.
kw: Behind the Greek is very likely the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus used (Mark 14:36). He shares with his disciples his own way of speaking to God.
A rare Greek word, hardly found outside the Lord's Prayer. It may mean “for today”, “for the coming day” or “needed for life”. The Church hears in it both ordinary bread and the Bread of Life.
Testing that could lead a person away from God. We ask the Father not to let us enter into a trial we cannot bear, and not to let us give way in it.
vv: Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.
Prayer is learned. The disciples did not think it came by itself, and they went to the right teacher.
Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
We begin with God and not with ourselves. To “hallow” the name is to let God be known as holy, in our words and in our lives.
And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us.
Luke speaks of sins in the first half and debts in the second. The forgiveness we ask and the forgiveness we give belong together.
ch: The Catechism notes that Luke gives five petitions and Matthew seven, and that the liturgy of the Church kept Matthew's text (CCC 2759). It quotes Tertullian, who called the Lord's Prayer a summary of the whole Gospel (CCC 2761). On the word “daily” it notes that the bread asked for is also the Bread of Life, the Body of Christ (CCC 2837).

qa: If Jesus was heard, why did he still die?

Hebrews says he prayed “to the one who was able to save him from death”. The Father did save him from death, not by keeping him from dying but by raising him on the third day. That is the answer our own prayers also share in: God does not always remove the cross, but he never leaves us in the grave.
rite: The Panchangam remembers Mar Seraphion today. In every hour of our daily prayer and before Communion in the Holy Qurbono we say the prayer the Lord taught, and we say it as sons and daughters who have learned it from the Son.
study: When have I prayed “with loud cries and tears”? How did God answer, even if not in the way I asked?
Which petition of the Our Father do I find hardest to mean? Why?

lead: Easter is not a place to stop. Hebrews urges believers to move on from the first lessons of faith toward maturity, and warns of ground that drinks the rain and yields only thorns. Luke tells of a friend who knocks at midnight and will not go away, and promises that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Growth comes from asking and receiving. The key words are perfection, rain and ask.

r.h: Let us go on toward perfection
set: Just before this passage the writer has scolded his hearers: by now they ought to be teachers, yet they still need milk and not solid food (5:11–14). So he resolves to lead them on. The six items he lists in 6:1–2 are the basics that a new Christian learned before and around Baptism.

Then comes one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, on those who have fallen away. It must be read with the verse that follows it: “Even though we speak in this way, beloved, we are confident of better things in your case” (6:9). The warning is meant to wake people up, not to drive them to despair.
str: vv. 1–3: move beyond the foundation, which has six parts.
vv. 4–6: the danger of falling away after receiving so much.
vv. 7–8: a picture from farming: the same rain, two kinds of ground.
kw: The state of the grown-up believer, able to take solid food. It is the same family of words used of Christ “made perfect” (5:9).

Early Christians used “enlightenment” as a name for Baptism. St Justin Martyr says so in the second century, and the Catechism repeats it (CCC 1216). The list in vv. 4–5 describes the gifts of Christian initiation.
Not an ordinary sin of weakness, but a deliberate turning away from Christ after knowing him, as if crucifying the Son of God again (6:6).
vv: Therefore let us go on toward perfection,
The writer says “let us”: he includes himself. Growth in faith is a road all of us walk together.
instruction about baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.
The “laying on of hands” was linked with the gift of the Spirit after Baptism (see Acts 8:17), the root of what our Church gives in Holy Mooron.
For it is impossible to restore again to repentance those who have once been enlightened,

Many Fathers, among them St John Chrysostom, read this as meaning that Baptism cannot be given a second time, not that repentance is closed (in substance). The person who refuses Christ cannot be brought back by human effort while he goes on refusing.
Ground that drinks up the rain falling on it repeatedly, and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God.
The rain is the same for both fields. What differs is the crop. Grace is given generously, and it asks for a harvest.
ch: The Church has always rejected the view that sins after Baptism cannot be forgiven. The Catechism says that there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive, and that the door of forgiveness stays open to all who turn back (CCC 982). It also teaches that Baptism is given once and cannot be repeated, because it marks the soul with a seal (CCC 1272). The passage is therefore a call to perseverance, and the sacrament of Penance is the Lord's answer to those who fall.

r.h: Ask, search, knock
set: Right after giving the Lord's Prayer, Jesus teaches how to pray it. In a village of his day, guests arrived at any hour, and hospitality was a duty for the whole community. A family's bread was baked for the day, and at night the house was shut, with the family sleeping together in one room. A friend who knocked would wake everyone.
Luke alone has the parable of the friend at midnight. The sayings that follow (vv. 9–13) are found also in Matthew 7:7–11.
str: vv. 5–8: the friend at midnight.
vv. 9–10: ask, search, knock.
vv. 11–13: from human fathers to the heavenly Father.
kw: Literally “shamelessness”. The man at the door does not stand on dignity. Jesus praises a prayer that is not too proud to keep knocking.
Three verbs in the present tense, which in Greek suggests going on doing them: keep asking, keep searching, keep knocking.
Where Matthew says the Father gives “good things” (Matthew 7:11), Luke says he gives the Holy Spirit. The best gift is God himself.
vv: Friend, lend me three loaves of bread;
He asks not for himself but for a guest. Prayer for others has a special place in this parable.
at least because of his persistence he will get up and give him whatever he needs.
The argument is from the lesser to the greater. If a sleepy neighbour gives in, how much more will God, who does not sleep and is not annoyed by our asking.
Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.
The verbs are passive in the first and third lines: “it will be given”, “will be opened”. The giver is God.
how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!
This is the promise of Pentecost, already spoken on the road to Jerusalem. In Qyomtho we ask for the Spirit day by day.
ch: The Catechism groups three parables of Luke on prayer: the friend at midnight, the widow and the judge, and the Pharisee and the tax collector (CCC 2613). St Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, explains that God does not need to be told our wants; he wants our desire to grow through prayer, so that we may be able to receive what he is ready to give (Letter 130, in substance).

qa: Does Hebrews 6 mean that a Christian who falls into serious sin cannot be forgiven?

No. The Church teaches that every sin can be forgiven to one who repents (CCC 982), and the Lord gave the sacrament of Penance for those who fall after Baptism. Hebrews warns about a hardened turning away from Christ. As long as a person refuses him, no one can bring that person back; but God's door is never shut to the one who knocks.
rite: Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae (Simeon bar Sabbae), bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the capital of the Persian empire, who was put to death with many companions under King Shapur II in the fourth century. The ancient accounts tell that he refused to force his people to pay a crushing double tax laid on Christians, and that an aged court official who had denied the faith repented on seeing him and died a martyr too. He is honoured by the Syriac Churches of East and West, and he is a living picture of Hebrews 6: the one who had fallen came back.
study: Since Easter, have I grown, or have I settled down? What one step toward maturity can I take this week?
For whom am I knocking at God's door at midnight? Do I keep knocking?

lead: Today Hebrews names the source of Christ's priesthood: not family descent but “the power of an indestructible life”, the life of the Risen One. Luke shows Jesus on his way to Jerusalem, where that life will pass through death, and someone asks him how many will be saved. He answers with a call: strive to enter through the narrow door. The key words are indestructible, approach and strive.

r.h: The power of an indestructible life
set: In 7:1–10 the writer has shown that Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him, stands above the priesthood of Levi. Now he draws the conclusion. Under the law of Moses the priests came from the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron. Jesus was of the tribe of Judah. If he is a priest, his priesthood must rest on something other than descent.
The writer speaks with deep respect of Israel's worship. His point is that God himself, in Psalm 110:4, had promised another priest, so the old order was always pointing beyond itself.
str: vv. 11–12: if the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would be needed.
vv. 13–14: our Lord came from Judah.
vv. 15–17: a priest by the power of an indestructible life.
vv. 18–19: a better hope, through which we approach God.
kw: Literally “that cannot be dissolved”. The life of the risen Christ is beyond the reach of death. This is the ground of his priesthood: “he always lives to make intercession” (7:25).
A legal word for cancelling an arrangement. Hebrews applies it to the rule that only descendants of Aaron could be priests, now that Christ has come.
The verb of worship. The whole purpose of priesthood is to let people come near to God, and in Christ this happens fully.
vv: For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah,
Hebrews takes for granted what the Gospels tell: Jesus was of the house of David, of the tribe of Judah (Matthew 1:1–3; Luke 1:27).
but through the power of an indestructible life.

Aaron's priesthood passed from father to son because every priest died. Christ's priesthood passes to no successor, because he lives for ever. Priests of the Church act in his person, not as his successors.
(for the law made nothing perfect); there is, on the other hand, the introduction of a better hope, through which we approach God.
The law was holy and good (Romans 7:12), but it could not by itself bring people to the goal. The “better hope” is Christ himself, the one through whom we draw near.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Old Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect, a first stage on the way to the Kingdom (CCC 1963). It also says that Christ is the one true Priest and that the ministerial priesthood makes his one priesthood present, quoting St Thomas Aquinas: only Christ is the true priest, the others being his ministers (CCC 1545). When a priest of our Church stands at the altar, it is Christ, alive for ever, who offers.

r.h: Strive to enter through the narrow door
set: Since 9:51 Luke has shown Jesus making his way to Jerusalem. Verse 22 reminds the reader of this journey: everything Jesus teaches along the road is said on the way to the Cross.
The question “will only a few be saved?” was discussed by teachers of the time. Jesus does not give a number. He turns a question about others into a call to the one who asked.
str: vv. 22–23: the journey and the question.
v. 24: strive to enter through the narrow door.
vv. 25–27: the shut door and the knocking from outside.
vv. 28–30: the banquet of the kingdom, with guests from every direction.
kw: From the word for an athletic contest, the root of our word “agony”. Entering the kingdom takes the whole of a person.
A door, not a road: there is a moment to go in. Jesus speaks of himself as the door elsewhere (John 10:9).
I do not know where you come from
The householder does not deny having seen them. He denies any real belonging, any bond of life with them.
vv: Lord, will only a few be saved?
A question of curiosity. Jesus does not answer the question of how many; he answers the question of how.
Strive to enter through the narrow door;
The door is open now. The effort asked is not to earn entry but to go in while the door stands open, by grace.
We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.
Being near Jesus is not the same as following him. Christians who eat at his table every Sunday hear this as a word to themselves.
Then people will come from east and west, from north and south, and will eat in the kingdom of God.
The prophets foresaw the nations gathering at God's feast (Isaiah 25:6). The table is wide, and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are already at it.
ch: This warning is addressed to those who heard Jesus in person, and through them to every disciple; it is not a judgement on any people. The Catechism takes up the Lord's call to “enter by the narrow gate” (Matthew 7:13–14) in its teaching on the last things, as an urgent call to conversion and responsibility (CCC 1036). The good news is in verse 29: the door is narrow, but the hall is full.

study: Christ's priesthood rests on “an indestructible life”. How does the Resurrection change the way I pray at the Holy Qurbono?
Do I ask questions about others' salvation more readily than I strive for my own? What would striving look like for me this week?

lead: On a Friday of Qyomtho the Church remembers the Passion in the light of the empty tomb. Hebrews explains the death of Christ as the blood of a new covenant, sealing God's promise as Moses once sealed the covenant at Sinai. Luke shows Jesus at a meal, telling guests to take the lowest place and hosts to invite those who cannot repay. The one who took the lowest place on the Cross is the host of the new covenant's table. The key words are covenant, blood and lowest place.

r.h: The mediator of a new covenant
set: Chapters 8–10 of Hebrews compare the worship of the first covenant with the work of Christ. Chapter 8 quoted at length Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). In 9:1–14 the writer described the tent of the old worship and the Day of Atonement, and said that Christ entered the true sanctuary “with his own blood” (9:12).
Today's verses explain why a death was needed. The writer uses the fact that one Greek word can mean both “covenant” and “will”, and then recalls the covenant ceremony at Sinai (Exodus 24:3–8).
str: v. 15: Christ the mediator; his death redeems.
vv. 16–17: a will takes effect only at death.
vv. 18–21: the first covenant was also sealed with blood.
v. 22: no forgiveness without the shedding of blood.
kw: In the Greek Old Testament this word translates the Hebrew bᵉrît, covenant. In ordinary Greek it meant a last will. Hebrews plays on both: God's promises come to us as an inheritance through the death of the Son.
One who stands between two parties and brings them together. Christ is mediator because he is both God and man (1 Timothy 2:5).
A word not found in any earlier Greek writing known to us. Behind it lies the teaching of Leviticus that “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11): blood offered means life given.
vv: For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance,
The goal is not only the removal of sin but an inheritance. Those who are called become heirs.
Hence not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
At Sinai, half the blood was thrown on the altar and half on the people (Exodus 24:6–8). God and people were bound together in one life.
This is the blood of the covenant that God has ordained for you.
Moses said “See the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). The form Hebrews gives, “This is”, is close to the Lord's words over the cup at the Supper (Mark 14:24).
without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
The writer states the principle of the old worship in order to show its fulfilment. The blood of animals pointed to the one gift of life that truly takes sin away.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the sacrifice of Christ is the sacrifice of the New Covenant, which restores us to communion with God through “the blood of the covenant” poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (CCC 613). In the Holy Qurbono the priest repeats the Lord's words over the cup, and the Church receives the blood of the new covenant as her Lord commanded.

r.h: Take the lowest place; invite the poor
set: Jesus has gone on a sabbath to eat at the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). He accepts the hospitality of Pharisees more than once in Luke (7:36; 11:37), and they are watching him closely. At such dinners guests reclined on couches arranged around the table, and the places nearest the host were the places of honour.
Jesus speaks first to the guests (vv. 7–11) and then to the host (vv. 12–14). What sounds like advice on manners is a parable about the kingdom.
str: vv. 7–11: to the guests: do not seek the first place.
vv. 12–14: to the host: invite those who cannot repay.
kw: Literally “first couch”. Seeking it was a way of claiming status in front of others.
The saying in v. 11 uses passives, “will be humbled”, “will be exalted”. It is God who does the lifting, as Mary sings: he “lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
The same root appears for repayment at the resurrection. God himself becomes the one who repays those who gave without return.
vv: When he noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, he told them a parable.
Luke calls it a parable. The table is an image of God's kingdom, where places are given, not grabbed.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
Jesus says it again after the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14). He lived it first, by taking the lowest place of all on the Cross.
But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind.
These are the very people the master brings in at the great dinner a few verses later (14:21).
for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.
Generosity that expects nothing in return is a sign of faith in the resurrection. We give now because we believe God will answer later.
ch: The Church reads this teaching as part of her preferential love for the poor. The Catechism says that God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor (CCC 2443), and that love for the poor belongs to the constant tradition of the Church (CCC 2444). Every gathering of Christians, from the parish feast to the family table, is measured by this Gospel.

study: Hebrews calls Christ's death the beginning of an inheritance. What does it mean to me that I am an heir of God's promises?
Whom could I invite, or help, this week who cannot repay me?

lead: Hebrews sets two pictures side by side: priests who stand day after day offering sacrifices again and again, and Christ who, after one offering, has sat down at God's right hand. Luke tells of a great dinner where everything is ready and the invited guests make excuses, so the host fills his house with the poor and with strangers from the roads. The sacrifice is complete, the table is set, and the invitation is still going out. This evening the Third Sunday after Qyomtho begins. The key words are single offering, ready and come.

r.h: By a single offering
set: This passage closes the long central section of Hebrews on Christ's priesthood and sacrifice (chapters 7–10). In 10:1–10 the writer has said that the law's sacrifices, repeated year after year, could not take away sin, and that Christ came to do the Father's will, offering his own body “once for all” (10:10).
Now the writer returns to the promise of Jeremiah 31 he quoted in chapter 8, and lets the Holy Spirit's own words close the argument.
str: v. 11: every priest stands, offering again and again.
vv. 12–14: Christ, after a single sacrifice, sat down.
vv. 15–17: the witness of the Spirit in Jeremiah's promise.
v. 18: where there is forgiveness, there is no longer an offering for sin.
kw: The offering of Christ on the Cross is one and is never repeated. Its effect reaches all times.
The Greek perfect tense describes an action complete in the past whose result lasts. What Christ did once remains effective.
The participle is present: “those who are being made holy”. The one sacrifice is finished; our sanctification goes on as we receive it.
vv: And every priest stands day after day at his service,
In the sanctuary of the old worship there was no seat for the priest. His work was never finished.
But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, “he sat down at the right hand of God,”
Sitting means the work is done, and it means royal authority (Psalm 110:1). The risen Christ reigns and intercedes.
For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are sanctified.
The whole of salvation is contained in this one sentence: one offering, all time, all who are being made holy.
Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
No new sacrifice can be added to Christ's. Every Christian offering is a sharing in his.
ch: The Catholic Church teaches that the Eucharist does not repeat or add to the sacrifice of the Cross, but makes that one sacrifice present. “The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice”, with the same victim and the same offerer, now offering through the ministry of priests (CCC 1367, following the Council of Trent). So when the Holy Qurbono is offered, the one sacrifice of Hebrews 10 is made present among us, and its fruits are given to us.

r.h: Come, for everything is ready now
set: The setting is still the sabbath meal at the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). One guest, hearing Jesus speak of the resurrection of the righteous, exclaims how blessed are those who will eat bread in the kingdom. Jesus answers with a parable that asks whether we will come when we are called.
In that world, a host sent a first invitation and then, when the meal was ready, a servant to call the guests. To refuse at the last moment was a public insult.
str: v. 15: a guest's exclamation.
vv. 16–17: the dinner and the call: “Come.”
vv. 18–20: three excuses.
vv. 21–23: the poor and the strangers brought in.
v. 24: the closing word.
kw: The main evening meal, here a feast. It is an image of the banquet of the kingdom that the prophets foretold (Isaiah 25:6).
To ask to be let off. All three excuses are polite, and all three put something good, land, oxen and marriage, before the host.
A strong word, but in the customs of the East it describes pressing an invitation on someone who is too humble to accept. The disciples at Emmaus “urged him strongly” in the same spirit (Luke 24:29).
vv: Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!
A pious wish about the future. Jesus turns it into a question about the present: you are invited now.
Come; for everything is ready now.
Everything has been prepared by the host. Nothing is asked of the guests except to come.
Go out at once into the streets and lanes of the town and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.
The same four groups Jesus told his host to invite (14:13). God does what he asks us to do.
and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.
The host wants a full house. The urgency is the urgency of love.
ch: The parable is a warning to every hearer, and first of all to the baptized, not to let good things keep us from God's table. It must never be read as God rejecting a whole people. Some in past centuries used “compel them to come in” to justify forcing people into the Church. The Church today teaches clearly that no one may be forced to embrace the faith against his will, because the act of faith is by its very nature voluntary (Dignitatis Humanae 10; CCC 160). The only compulsion the Gospel knows is the pressure of a warm invitation.

qa: If Christ's sacrifice is complete, why do we offer the Holy Qurbono every day?

Not to add to the Cross, but to receive it. The one sacrifice of Christ is made present in the Holy Qurbono, so that each generation can share in it and receive its fruit (CCC 1366–1367). Hebrews says there is no other offering for sin; the Holy Qurbono is not another one but the same, offered in the way the Lord commanded at the Supper.
study: Christ “sat down” because his work was finished. Where am I still trying to earn what he has already given?
Which of the three excuses sounds most like mine? What is keeping me from the Lord's table?

lead: The Third Sunday after Qyomtho gathers its readings around a road and a table. The Evening Gospel (Mark 16:9–13) tells in a few lines how the risen Lord “appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country”. Exodus 40:1–15 shows Moses setting up the tabernacle and anointing Aaron and his sons, so that God may dwell among his people. In Joshua 2:1–14 Rahab, an outsider, shelters the spies and confesses the God of Israel. Amos 4:6–13 repeats five times God's sad refrain, “yet you did not return to me”. In Acts 4:5–22 Peter and John, “uneducated and ordinary men”, tell the council, “we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

We study three more closely. Isaiah hears God say, “Here I am, here I am,” to people who were not looking for him. Ephesians tells the baptized that they were dead and have been raised with Christ, by grace. Luke tells how the risen Jesus walked with two disciples who did not recognize him, opened the Scriptures to them, and was known in the breaking of the bread. The key words are found, grace and recognize.

r.h: I was ready to be found
set: Many scholars think that chapters 56–66 of Isaiah speak to the community in Judah after the return from exile in Babylon, in the late sixth century before Christ. The temple was being rebuilt, hopes were high, and the people were divided. Some still followed old pagan rites. Chapter 64 ended with the people's anguished prayer: “Will you keep silent, and punish us so severely?” (64:12). Chapter 65 is God's answer.
The answer begins with a surprise. God has not been hiding. He has been calling out all along, even to those who never called to him.
str: v. 1: God ready to be sought and found, saying “Here I am”.
v. 2: hands held out all day to a rebellious people.
vv. 3–5: the rites they practised and their claim to be holier than others.
vv. 6–7: God will not keep silent but will judge.
kw: I was ready to be sought, to be found
The Hebrew forms mean “I let myself be sought”, “I let myself be found”. God takes the first step, and makes himself available before anyone looks for him.
In the Bible this is usually a person's answer to God: Abraham says it (Genesis 22:1), and Isaiah himself, “Here am I; send me!” (6:8). Here God says it, twice, to people who have not called.
A people who turn aside, stubborn like a wayward child (see Deuteronomy 21:18). The word describes the conduct of those who follow their own devices, not the worth of a nation.
vv: I was ready to be sought out by those who did not ask, to be found by those who did not seek me.
Grace comes before our searching. The two disciples on the road to Emmaus were not looking for the risen Lord; he came to them.
I held out my hands all day long to a rebellious people,

The picture is of open arms, waiting. St Justin Martyr and other early Christian writers saw in it the arms of the Lord stretched out on the Cross (First Apology 35, in substance). Those arms are held out to every person.
who sit inside tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat swine’s flesh,
These seem to be practices of consulting the dead and of pagan ritual meals, forbidden by the law (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 18:11). People sought life among the dead.
who say, “Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.”
Those who had turned away from God still claimed a holiness that set them above others. False religion makes people proud and keeps them apart.
ch: St Paul quotes these verses in Romans 10:20–21: he hears verse 1 of the nations who found God without seeking him, and verse 2 of Israel, to whom God's hands remained stretched out. Paul goes on at once: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). The Church reads Isaiah 65 in that spirit, as a word about God's patient love for all, and as a warning to every believer, never as a judgement on the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The God who says “Here I am” is the God who comes to meet the disciples on the road.

r.h: By grace you have been saved
set: The Letter to the Ephesians has long been received as a letter of St Paul. Many scholars today think it was written by a disciple of his in his name, drawing on his teaching; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church reads it as inspired Scripture in either case. It may have been meant for several churches in the region of Ephesus.

Chapter 1 ended by praising the power God showed when “he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand” (1:20). Chapter 2 says that the same power has worked in the baptized. What God did for Christ, he has done for us with him.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead, following the course of this world.
vv. 4–7: “But God”: made alive, raised and seated with Christ.
vv. 8–10: saved by grace through faith, created for good works.
kw: by grace you have been saved
The Greek perfect tense means saved and remaining in that state. The source is grace, God's undeserved favour.
made alive with, raised with, seated with
Three verbs joined with “with” (syn). Christians share Christ's own life, Resurrection and glory. Baptism is the moment of this union (see Colossians 2:12).
God's handiwork, his work of art. Our English word “poem” comes from this Greek word. The Christian life is something God creates.
vv: You were dead through the trespasses and sins
Not weak or sick, but dead. Only someone who gives life can help the dead, and that is what the next verses describe.
But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us
The turning point of the passage. All of salvation hangs on these two words, “But God”.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
Faith is the hand that receives; grace is the gift. Even faith itself is God's gift.
For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works,
Our own works cannot earn the grace that saves; good works are the purpose for which God has made us new. Grace that saves also makes us able to do good.
ch: The Catholic Church teaches that justification comes from the grace of God, given to us at Baptism, and that no one can merit the first grace of conversion (CCC 1996, 2010). It also teaches that the good works of the justified are truly good and pleasing to God, because they are the fruit of his grace in us: “The charity of Christ is the source in us of all our merits before God” (CCC 2011). Ephesians 2:8–10 holds both together: we are saved by grace, and created for good works.

r.h: Known in the breaking of the bread
set: It is still Easter Day. In the morning the women found the tomb empty and heard the angels (24:1–12). The apostles thought their report “an idle tale” (24:11). That afternoon two disciples, one named Cleopas, walk out of Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus. Luke alone tells this story at length; the Evening Gospel shows that Mark's longer ending knew it in brief.

Where Emmaus lay is not certain. Most manuscripts give the distance as sixty stadia, “about seven miles”, while some give one hundred and sixty. Several places have been proposed, among them Emmaus-Nicopolis (Amwas), El-Qubeibeh and others, and pilgrims honour more than one.
str: vv. 13–16: the two on the road; Jesus joins them, unrecognized.
vv. 17–24: their story: hope lost and a puzzling report.
vv. 25–27: Jesus opens the Scriptures.
vv. 28–32: “Stay with us”; the breaking of the bread; eyes opened.
vv. 33–35: back to Jerusalem: “The Lord has risen indeed.”
kw: Their eyes “were kept” from recognizing him. The passive suggests that God was at work: recognition would come as a gift, at the right moment.
The key verb of the chapter. Their eyes were opened (v. 31), he opened the Scriptures (v. 32), and he opened the minds of the Eleven (v. 45). The risen Lord opens what was closed.
The phrase of v. 35, which Luke uses again of the first Christians' gatherings (Acts 2:42). It became one of the earliest names for the Eucharist (CCC 1329).
vv: but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
The Lord is present before he is recognized. Much of the Christian life is learning to see one who is already beside us.
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel.
The saddest sentence in the story, in the past tense. Jesus does not mock their disappointment; he walks with it and listens.
Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and then enter into his glory?
“Necessary” is the necessity of God's plan, foretold in the Scriptures. The Cross was not the end of the hope but the way to it.
Then beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them the things about himself in all the scriptures.
The first Christian Bible study, given by the Lord himself. The whole Old Testament is read with Christ as its key.
he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them.
The same four actions as at the feeding of the crowd (9:16) and at the Last Supper (22:19). The guest has become the host.
Were not our hearts burning within us while he was talking to us on the road, while he was opening the scriptures to us?
Only after recognizing him at table do they understand what was happening on the road. Word and table belong together.
ch: The Catechism sees in Emmaus the shape of the Eucharistic celebration: the Lord walks with his people, opens the Scriptures, then takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it (CCC 1347). The Second Vatican Council says that the Church has always venerated the Scriptures as she has venerated the Body of the Lord, offering the bread of life from the one table of the Word and of the Body of Christ (Dei Verbum 21). St Augustine told his people that the disciples did not recognize the Lord while he explained the Scriptures, but did in the breaking of bread, and that we too, who do not see him in the flesh, know him there (Sermon 235, in substance).

qa: Why did the two disciples not recognize Jesus?

Luke says that “their eyes were kept from recognizing him”, which suggests that God was at work. Mark's Evening Gospel says he appeared “in another form”. The risen body of Christ is truly his own, but glorified, and he is known only when he gives himself to be known. Recognition came through the Scriptures opened and the bread broken, the way by which we too come to know him.
Was the meal at Emmaus a Eucharist?

Luke tells it with the same words he used at the Last Supper: he took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it. Many Fathers and the Church read the scene as Eucharistic, and the Catechism uses it to explain the shape of the liturgy (CCC 1347). Whether or not we call that evening meal a Qurbono in the full sense, Luke clearly wanted his readers to recognize the Lord where they broke bread every Sunday.
Does Ephesians 2:9, “not the result of works”, mean good works do not matter?

No. Verse 10 says that we were created “for good works”. Paul's point is that no one earns salvation; it is God's gift. Once given, grace bears fruit, and the good works we do in Christ are pleasing to God and have their reward, because they are his grace at work in us (CCC 2011).
rite: The Syro-Malankara Sunday follows the same road as Emmaus. In the Holy Qurbono the Word is read first, ending with the Gospel proclaimed by the celebrant; then comes the anaphora, in which the priest repeats the Lord's words over the bread and the cup, and the fraction, when the Body of the Lord is broken. Every Sunday of Qyomtho we walk with Cleopas and his companion from the Scriptures to the table. The evening prayer of Saturday, with today's Evening Gospel from Mark, already set us on the road.
study: When have I been walking away from Jerusalem, saying “we had hoped”? How did the Lord come alongside me?
God says “Here I am” to those who did not seek him. Who in my life is not seeking God, and how might I show them his open arms?
Ephesians says I am God's handiwork, created for good works. What good work has God prepared for me this week?
How can I prepare to hear the Word and receive the bread at next Sunday's Holy Qurbono so that my heart burns within me?

lead: In the week after the Emmaus Sunday the Church reads on in the Letter to the Hebrews. Monday opens its great call to come near: by the blood of Jesus the way into God's presence stands open, so let us approach, hold fast and keep meeting together. Luke tells the same truth as a story. A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after one sheep and carries it home rejoicing. One reading shows the door that has been opened, the other the shepherd who goes looking for those still outside it.

r.h: A new and living way
set: Hebrews does not name its author. The Church has always received it with the letters of St Paul, though since the early centuries many have thought that another hand, perhaps one of Paul's companions, wrote it. It is addressed to Christians who were growing tired and were tempted to drift away. Chapters 7 to 10 have shown at length that Christ is the high priest who entered the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood (9:11–12). Today's passage turns that teaching into encouragement. It begins with “Therefore”: everything argued so far now becomes a reason to act.
str: vv. 19–21: what we have: confidence to enter, a new and living way, a great priest.
v. 22: let us approach.
v. 23: let us hold fast.
vv. 24–25: let us consider one another, and keep meeting together.
¶ The three calls follow the order of faith (v. 22), hope (v. 23) and love (v. 24).
kw: Openness, boldness. In a Greek city it was the right of a citizen to speak openly in the assembly. Here it is the right of children to enter their Father's house without fear. The word returns in 10:35.

The veil that closed off the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). The writer calls Christ's flesh the curtain: his humanity, given up on the Cross, is the way through. The Gospels record that at his death the curtain of the temple was torn in two (Mark 15:38).
Assembling, gathering; the word is related to “synagogue”. The writer means the gathering of Christians for worship, which some among them had already stopped attending.
vv: by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (that is, through his flesh),
The way is “new”, freshly made, and “living”, because it is not a road of stones but a person. Jesus said of himself, “I am the way” (John 14:6).
let us approach with a true heart in full assurance of faith,

The rest of the verse speaks of hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water. The sprinkling recalls the consecration of priests (Exodus 29:21), and the washing most likely recalls Baptism. Those who have been washed may come near.
Let us hold fast to the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who has promised is faithful.
Our steadiness rests on God's faithfulness, not on our feelings.
not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.
“The Day” is the day of the Lord's coming. The nearer it draws, the more the assembly matters, not the less.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it explains why Christians gather on Sunday: the practice of the Christian assembly goes back to the apostolic age, and Hebrews reminds the faithful not to neglect to meet together (CCC 2178). The Church sees in the opened curtain the meaning of her worship. In the Holy Qurbono the faithful do not stand outside; they are led by their high priest into the presence of the Father, and they receive the Body and Blood through which the way was opened.

r.h: Until he finds it
set: Luke 15 holds three parables of things lost and found: a sheep, a coin and a son. They are told in answer to a complaint. Tax collectors, who gathered taxes for Rome or for local rulers and were widely thought dishonest, and others known as sinners, came to listen to Jesus, and he shared their table. The Pharisees and scribes were serious teachers of the Law, and to them sharing a meal meant approval. Jesus does not deny that these people are lost. He says that God goes looking for them.
str: vv. 1–2: who comes near, and who grumbles.
vv. 3–6: the parable: the search, the shoulders, the celebration.
v. 7: the meaning: joy in heaven over one who repents.
kw: The word the Greek Bible uses for Israel's muttering in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2). Grumbling against God's generosity is an old temptation.
To receive someone as a guest. The complaint is true, and it is the heart of the Gospel.
Joy returns at the end of each of the three parables (15:7, 10, 32). The chapter is about the joy of God.
vv: go after the one that is lost until he finds it?
“Until he finds it.” The shepherd does not search for a while and then give up. Ezekiel had promised that God himself would seek out the lost (Ezekiel 34:11–16).
When he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders and rejoices.

There is no scolding. St Gregory the Great says that the shepherd laid the sheep on his shoulders because Christ, taking up our human nature, carried our sins himself (Homilies on the Gospels 34, in substance). Some of the earliest Christian paintings, in the Roman catacombs, show this very picture.
there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
“Heaven” is a reverent way of saying God. Many read the words about the ninety-nine as gentle irony, since all need repentance. The point is how much one returning person matters to God.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545), and that by receiving them at his table he showed that forgiveness brings a person back into the community of God's people (CCC 1443). The Church reads the parable as the pattern of the Sacrament of Reconciliation and of all pastoral care: the shepherd's work is to go out, and the welcome home is a feast, not a trial.

qa: Does God care less for the ninety-nine?

No. The shepherd leaves them in the wilderness because he is sure of them, and he will bring the found sheep back to the same flock. The parable does not measure God's love; it shows its direction. Matthew's form of it ends: it is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should be lost (Matthew 18:14).
study: Hebrews says that some had made a habit of staying away from the assembly. Who from my parish or family has stopped coming, and what could I do this week to encourage them?
Do I grumble, even quietly, when God's mercy reaches someone I think does not deserve it?

lead: Tuesday sets two hard sayings side by side. Hebrews warns those who have known Christ not to turn their backs on him on purpose, and Luke gathers sayings of Jesus about money, the Law and marriage. Neither reading lets faith become a matter of words alone. What we have received must shape what we choose.

r.h: Do not spurn the blood of the covenant
set: The encouragement of 10:19–25 is followed at once by a warning, as happened earlier in the letter (6:4–8). The writer speaks to people who have been baptized and are tempted to give up the faith altogether and go back, perhaps under pressure from outside. He does not speak of the ordinary weakness of believers, but of a deliberate turning away from Christ.
str: vv. 26–27: deliberate sin after knowing the truth leaves no other sacrifice.
vv. 28–29: from the lesser to the greater: if the Law of Moses was serious, how much more the covenant in Christ's blood.
vv. 30–31: two sayings from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:35–36), and the conclusion.
kw: Deliberately; and the verb that follows is in a tense of continuing action, which the NRSV renders “persist”. The writer has in mind not weakness but a settled choice to reject Christ, as v. 29 describes.
Literally “trampled underfoot”. It pictures treating the Son of God as worthless.
The Spirit who gives grace. To insult him is to refuse the very gift that heals.
vv: For if we willfully persist in sin after having received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,
The sentence does not say that God refuses to forgive. It says that if Christ's sacrifice is rejected, there is no other to turn to, since the old sacrifices have been fulfilled in his.
profaned the blood of the covenant by which they were sanctified, and outraged the Spirit of grace?
The Son, the blood of his covenant and the Spirit: the sin in view is turning against the whole gift of God.
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

David once chose to fall into the hand of the Lord rather than into human hands, because his mercy is great (2 Samuel 24:14). The same hands are fearful to those who despise him and a refuge to those who turn back.
ch: In the third century the followers of Novatian used verses like these to say that Christians who had denied the faith under persecution could never be received back. The Church rejected this. St Ambrose, writing On Penance against them, defended the Church's power to forgive the repentant (in substance), and the Catechism teaches that there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive (CCC 982). The sin that cannot be forgiven is the one that refuses to repent and so refuses God's mercy (CCC 1864). The warning is real, and it is given so that no one reaches that point.

r.h: You cannot serve God and wealth
set: These verses follow the parable of the dishonest manager (16:1–8), and Luke gathers several sayings around it. The thread is faithfulness: with money, with the Law, and in marriage. Luke notes that some Pharisees who heard this “were lovers of money” and ridiculed Jesus. He is describing those listeners, not the Pharisees as a whole, many of whom were devout; Luke also tells of Pharisees who warned Jesus of danger (13:31).
str: vv. 11–13: faithfulness with money, and the two masters.
vv. 14–15: the ridicule, and God who knows the heart.
vv. 16–17: the Law and the prophets, and the kingdom.
v. 18: marriage.
kw: An Aramaic word for property or riches. Jesus speaks of it almost as a rival lord, which is why older translations kept the name “mammon”.
A strong biblical word for what is repugnant to God, often used of idols. To prize wealth above God is a kind of idolatry.
Literally “a little horn”: the tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.
vv: You cannot serve God and wealth.
A slave belonged wholly to one owner. Jesus does not say “should not” but “cannot”.
but God knows your hearts;
Public reputation and God's knowledge are set side by side. What counts is what he sees.
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one stroke of a letter in the law to be dropped.
The kingdom does not cancel the Law; it fulfils it. The very next verse shows Jesus asking more than the practice of his day, not less.
Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery,
Luke gives the saying with no exception (compare Mark 10:11–12). Moses had allowed a certificate of divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1); Jesus goes back to the beginning (Mark 10:6–9).
ch: The Catechism lists money among the things that can become an idol when honoured in place of God (CCC 2113), and it quotes “You cannot serve God and mammon” against any system that makes profit the only rule (CCC 2424). On marriage it teaches that the Lord insisted on the original intention of the Creator, who willed that marriage be indissoluble (CCC 2382). It also notes that one spouse may be the innocent victim of a divorce (CCC 2386); the Church is called to stand beside those who suffer when a marriage breaks.

qa: What does “everyone tries to enter it by force” mean?

The Greek verb biazetai is hard to translate, and Matthew has a similar saying (Matthew 11:12). It may mean that people press eagerly into the kingdom, or that they are strongly urged to enter it. Scholars are divided. What is clear is that since John the Baptist something new is happening: the good news of the kingdom is being proclaimed.
study: Is there a part of my life where I have quietly decided not to let Christ in? What would it mean to bring it to him in Confession?
Where does money compete with God for my loyalty: in time, in worry, in what I am proud of?

lead: Wednesday asks how faith lasts. Hebrews tells tired Christians to remember the early days of their faith, when they suffered with joy, and not to throw away their confidence now. In Luke the apostles hear what forgiveness asks, seven times in a day, and they do the right thing: they ask for more faith. Jesus answers that the question is not how much faith, but whether it is real.

r.h: Do not abandon your confidence
set: After the warning of vv. 26–31 comes encouragement. The readers had once endured public insult; some of them had been imprisoned, and others had lost their property. The letter gives no names or dates. Its closing greeting from “those from Italy” (13:24) suggests a link with Rome, and many scholars connect these sufferings with troubles faced by Christians there in the first century, but certainty is not possible.
str: vv. 32–34: remember the former days.
vv. 35–36: do not abandon your confidence; you need endurance.
vv. 37–39: the word of the prophet (Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3–4), and “we are not among those who shrink back”.
kw: Also used at 6:4. Early Christians called Baptism “enlightenment”; St Justin Martyr uses this name in the second century (First Apology 61).
Not passive waiting but steady staying power under a heavy load.
Drawing back in fear. It is the opposite of parrēsia, the confidence of v. 35.
vv: But recall those earlier days when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,
Memory is a remedy for weariness. What God did in us at the beginning is a pledge of what he will do.
you cheerfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you yourselves possessed something better and more lasting.
Their joy did not come from loss itself but from knowing what could not be taken away.
but my righteous one will live by faith.
Habakkuk 2:4, quoted in its Greek form. Paul also uses it (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Here faith means faithful perseverance while waiting for the Lord.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith can be lost, and that to persevere in it to the end we must nourish it with the word of God and beg the Lord to increase our faith (CCC 162). The Church has always seen in passages like this one a call to remember: the anniversaries of Baptism, the witness of those who suffered before us, and above all the memorial of the Lord in the Holy Qurbono.

r.h: Increase our faith
set: Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem that Luke describes from 9:51 onward. He has just told the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31). Now he turns to his disciples with short teachings: on causing others to stumble, on correcting and forgiving, and on faith.
str: vv. 1–2: causing others to stumble.
vv. 3–4: rebuke, and forgive without limit.
vv. 5–6: “Increase our faith!” and the mustard seed.
kw: Originally the trigger of a trap or an obstacle that makes someone fall. Here, anything that leads another person into sin.
To correct, to warn seriously. Forgiveness in this passage does not mean pretending that nothing happened.
Usually identified with the black mulberry, a tree with deep, strong roots. To tell it to be planted in the sea is a deliberate impossibility.
vv: It would be better for you if a millstone were hung around your neck and you were thrown into the sea than for you to cause one of these little ones to stumble.
“Little ones” are not only children but the weak and those new in faith.
If another disciple sins, you must rebuke the offender, and if there is repentance, you must forgive.
The Greek says “your brother”. Correction is part of love, and forgiveness answers repentance.
The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!”
Faced with a command they cannot keep alone, they pray. Jesus' answer shows that even a little real faith, faith in God and not in ourselves, can do what seems impossible.
ch: The Catechism says that there is no limit or measure to this forgiveness, which is divine in its very nature (CCC 2845). It admits that it is not in our power to stop feeling an offence or to forget it, but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion (CCC 2843). The apostles' prayer, “Increase our faith”, is the right response to every command of Christ that seems too great for us.

study: What do I remember of the early days of my faith, or of a time when God was very close? How can that memory help me now?
Is there someone I must forgive “seven times”? Can I make the apostles' prayer my own today?

lead: Thursday's readings are about not losing heart. In the NRSV both use the same words: Hebrews tells us to consider Jesus “so that you may not grow weary or lose heart” (12:3), and Luke introduces the parable of the widow with “their need to pray always and not to lose heart” (18:1). One reading points to the runners who have finished before us and to Jesus at the finish; the other to a woman who would not stop asking.

r.h: Looking to Jesus
set: Chapter 11 has just listed the heroes of faith, from Abel to the prophets and martyrs, and ended by saying that they “did not receive what was promised” (11:39). Now the writer draws the conclusion with “Therefore”. The picture is a stadium: the runners on the track, the crowd around them, the finishing line ahead.
str: v. 1: surrounded by witnesses, lay aside every weight and run.
v. 2: look to Jesus, who endured the Cross and is now seated at God's right hand.
v. 3: consider him, so as not to grow weary.
kw: A great crowd. They are witnesses first because they bore witness to God by their lives; the picture of spectators watching a race is also present.
A contest, a struggle; the word from which “agony” comes. The Christian life is pictured as an athletic contest that needs endurance.
Jesus is the one who goes ahead and opens the way, and the one who brings faith to its goal. He has run the whole course himself.
vv: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses,
The saints are not distant figures but companions who have finished their race and now encourage ours.
who for the sake of the joy that was set before him endured the cross, disregarding its shame,

The small Greek word anti can mean “for the sake of” or “instead of”. The NRSV takes the first: he endured for the joy ahead. Others read it as: he set aside the joy that was his and chose the Cross, and the Malayalam Bible follows this reading. Both are true of Christ (Philippians 2:6–8).
Consider him who endured such hostility against himself from sinners,
The cure for weariness is not to look at ourselves but at him.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of the witnesses of faith: we must turn to them, and above all to Jesus, “the pioneer and perfecter of our faith” (CCC 165). It also teaches that the witnesses who have gone before us into the Kingdom, especially those the Church recognizes as saints, share in the living tradition of prayer and pray for us (CCC 2683).

r.h: Pray always and do not lose heart
set: The parable follows Jesus' teaching on the coming of the Son of Man (17:20–37). Luke tells us its meaning before he tells the story. In Israel a widow was the classic example of a person without protection, and the Law commanded special care for widows (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18). Judges were to judge fairly and take no bribes (Deuteronomy 16:18–20). This judge, Jesus says, neither feared God nor had respect for people (18:2).
str: v. 1: the purpose of the parable.
vv. 2–5: the judge and the widow.
vv. 6–8a: the lesson: how much more will God do justice.
v. 8b: the question about faith.
kw: To grow weary, to give up. Paul uses the same verb when he says, “we do not lose heart” (2 Corinthians 4:16).
Give a just verdict for me, vindicate me. She is not asking for revenge but for her rights.
Literally “strike under the eye”, a boxing term (Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 9:27). The judge says, half in jest, that she will end up giving him a black eye.
vv: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
The parable is not about wearing God down. It is about our need: we stop praying before God stops listening.
And will not God grant justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night?
The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. If even this judge gives in, how much more will God, who is just and who loves his chosen ones.
And yet, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?”
The question turns back on the hearer. God's faithfulness is not in doubt; ours is.
ch: The Catechism names this as one of the three chief parables on prayer in Luke, centred on one quality of prayer: we must pray always, without ceasing, with the patience of faith (CCC 2613). The Syriac Churches have always loved praying through the day; in our tradition the Shehimo, the prayer of the hours, is one way of answering this command to pray always.

study: What “weight” do I need to lay aside so that I can run more lightly toward Christ?
For what intention have I stopped praying because the answer seemed slow? Can I take it up again this week?

lead: Today our Church keeps the feast of Mar Geevarghese Sahada, St George the Martyr, a Christian soldier who gave his life for Christ in the persecution of the early fourth century and whose tomb at Lydda in Palestine was soon a place of pilgrimage. The weekday reading of Hebrews gives way to two readings chosen for a martyr.

In the Epistle, Paul, near the end of his own life, gives Timothy three pictures of the Christian: the soldier who pleases the one who enlisted him, the athlete who competes by the rules, and the farmer who works. In the Gospel, Jesus sends his disciples out like sheep among wolves, warns them that they will be handed over, and promises that the Spirit of the Father will speak through them. Read in the season of Qyomtho, both readings say the same thing: a martyr is a witness to the risen Lord. The key words are soldier, testimony and endurance.

r.h: A good soldier of Christ Jesus
set: The Second Letter to Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome near the end of his life (1:8, 17; 4:6–8). Timothy, his younger co-worker, has been left in charge of the Church at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3). Many scholars today think that the Pastoral Letters were written by a disciple in Paul's name after his death; others, with the long tradition of the Church, hold that they come from Paul himself, perhaps with the help of a secretary. Either way the Church receives them as inspired Scripture, and their picture of Paul's last charge is precious.

Paul often uses the images of soldier and athlete. He calls Epaphroditus his “fellow soldier” (Philippians 2:25), describes the armour of God (Ephesians 6:10–17), and compares himself to a runner and a boxer in training (1 Corinthians 9:24–27). In the same chapter of 1 Corinthians he asks who serves as a soldier at his own expense, or plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit (9:7).
str: v. 1: be strong in grace.
v. 2: hand on what you have received.
vv. 3–4: the soldier.
v. 5: the athlete.
v. 6: the farmer.
¶ The next verse adds: “Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things” (2:7). The three pictures are meant to be pondered, not just admired.
kw: One Greek word: “suffer hardship together with”. Timothy's sufferings are joined to Paul's, and both are joined to Christ's (compare 1:8).
The one who enlisted the soldier. A soldier does not choose his commander; he is chosen. The Christian is enlisted by Christ in Baptism.

At the games an athlete had to keep the rules of training and of the contest to win the crown. The crown, stephanos, was a wreath; the Church speaks of the martyr's crown, and the first martyr's own name, Stephen, means “crown”.
