vv: You then, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus;
The verb is passive in form: “be strengthened”. Strength comes first from grace, not from will power.
and what you have heard from me through many witnesses entrust to faithful people who will be able to teach others as well.

Four links in one chain: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others. The verb is the one used for placing something in safekeeping, as with “the good treasure entrusted to you” (1:14). This is what Tradition means: handing on.
Share in suffering like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
Paul does not promise Timothy an easy life. He invites him to share the hardship that Paul himself is bearing in chains.
No one serving in the army gets entangled in everyday affairs; the soldier’s aim is to please the enlisting officer.
Not a rejection of ordinary life, but a matter of first loyalty. A soldier does not let other concerns decide where he stands.
It is the farmer who does the work who ought to have the first share of the crops.
The last picture is the quietest: patient labour, and a harvest that comes later.
ch: The Fathers loved this picture. St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom, wrote to St Polycarp that Christians should please the one under whom they serve as soldiers, and let none be found a deserter; let Baptism be their weapons, faith their helmet, love their spear, endurance their armour (Letter to Polycarp 6, in substance). The Church has many soldier saints, and Mar Geevarghese is the best loved of them in the East.

The Second Vatican Council says that the Church considers martyrdom an exceptional gift and the highest proof of love, by which the disciple is made like the Master (Lumen Gentium 42). Verse 2 is also read as a witness to the apostolic succession: the apostles handed on to their successors what they had received, so that the Gospel would be kept whole and alive in the Church (CCC 77).

r.h: Sheep in the midst of wolves
set: Matthew 10 is the mission discourse. Jesus names the Twelve and sends them first “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:5–6). In our passage the horizon widens: the disciples will stand “before governors and kings” and bear witness “to them and the Gentiles” (10:18). Mark places similar words in Jesus' teaching about the end (Mark 13:9–13). The warnings reach beyond the first mission to the whole life of the Church.

When Jesus speaks of councils and “their synagogues”, he is speaking of the world his first disciples knew. They were Jews preaching to fellow Jews, and the first conflicts were quarrels within one family of faith. The passage does not accuse a people. Persecution comes from many sides: from governors and kings, who were Gentile rulers, and even from one's own household (10:21).
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves; wise and innocent.
vv. 17–20: handed over, and the Spirit who speaks.
vv. 21–22: division in families, and endurance to the end.
v. 23: flee to the next town.
vv. 24–25: the disciple will be like the teacher.
kw: Prudent like a serpent, which knows danger, and without guile like a dove, literally “unmixed”, with nothing false in it. The disciple needs both: neither naive nor cunning.
From martys, witness, the word that became “martyr”. The Syriac word sahdo, in our Malayalam sahada, means the same: a witness. The martyrs are those whose testimony was sealed with their blood.
From hypomonē, steady staying power. It is the same word family that Hebrews uses for the endurance of Christ (Hebrews 12:2).
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
The Shepherd sends sheep, not wolves. Their strength is not in their own claws.
and you will be dragged before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them and the Gentiles.
Even arrest becomes a pulpit. Many of the martyrs' acts record a confession of faith made before a judge.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
This is the only place in Matthew where the Spirit is called “the Spirit of your Father”. The disciples are not alone in court; the Father speaks for his children.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Salvation is not promised to the fearless but to those who remain. Endurance is itself a gift of grace.
A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above the master;
What happened to Jesus will happen to his own. If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, a name for the prince of demons (12:24), they will not spare his household.
ch: St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, says that as long as we are sheep we conquer, even when surrounded by many wolves; but if we become wolves we are beaten, because the help of the Shepherd leaves us (Homilies on Matthew 33, in substance). Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed (Apology 50, in substance): the Church grew where the martyrs died.

The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473). It adds that the Church has gathered with great care the records of those who persevered to the end (CCC 2474). The martyr's feast belongs in the season of the Resurrection, because no one gives his life for a story he thinks is untrue.

qa: How much do we really know about St George?

The core is firm: he was a Christian soldier martyred in the great persecution of the early fourth century, most likely under the emperor Diocletian, and his tomb at Lydda (Diospolis), where St Peter once healed Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35), was honoured very early. The long stories of his tortures, and the dragon, came later; the dragon is best read as a picture of the old enemy whom every faithful Christian strikes down. The Roman calendar too keeps his memorial on this day. We honour him for what is certain: he chose Christ.
Does Jesus tell us to seek martyrdom?

No. In v. 23 he says, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.” The Church has never praised those who rashly hand themselves over. The account of St Polycarp's martyrdom tells of a man named Quintus who gave himself up, and then lost courage, and it says that the Gospel does not teach this (Martyrdom of Polycarp 4, in substance). Martyrdom is a gift received when there is no faithful way out, not a goal to be pursued.
Can a Christian serve as a soldier?

Yes. The Catechism says that those who serve their country in the armed forces are servants of the security and freedom of nations, and that if they carry out their duty honourably they truly contribute to the common good and the maintenance of peace (CCC 2310). St George's witness was not that he left the army but that, as a soldier, he would not deny Christ.
rite: In the Syriac tradition St George is Mar Giwargis, and the title sahdo, Sahada in our usage, is given to the martyrs: it simply means witness. The Panchangam keeps his feast today, and across Kerala churches of several traditions are dedicated to him and countless families carry his name. In the Holy Qurbono the Church remembers the saints and martyrs before the altar, and the feast of a martyr in Qyomtho is itself an Easter feast: we honour Mar Geevarghese because Christ is risen, and pray for those who suffer for the name of Jesus in many lands today.
study: Paul gives three pictures: the soldier, the athlete, the farmer. Which one describes what Christ is asking of me at this time of my life?
Who in my life has handed on the faith to me, as Paul to Timothy? To whom am I handing it on?
Jesus asks us to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Where do I tend to be naive, and where do I tend to be cunning?
If I bear the name Geevarghese, Varghese or George, or love this saint, what small act of courage for Christ can I offer today?

lead: Saturday closes the week with two lessons in humility before God. Hebrews asks Christians to accept hardship as a father's training and to pursue peace and holiness. In Luke two men pray in the temple, and only one goes home justified. Both readings ask who will see the Lord: the one who lets God correct him, and the one who asks for mercy.

r.h: The Lord disciplines those whom he loves
set: The readers have suffered, but “not yet” to the point of blood (v. 4). The writer helps them to understand their hardships by quoting Proverbs 3:11–12. In the ancient world it was taken for granted that a good father trains his children, with teaching and correction together. The writer does not say that every suffering is a punishment for a particular sin (compare John 9:3). He says that God can use every hardship to form his children.
str: v. 4: the struggle against sin.
vv. 5–6: the word of Proverbs.
vv. 7–11: discipline as a father's training, and its peaceful fruit.
vv. 12–13: strengthen weak knees, make straight paths.
vv. 14–17: pursue peace and holiness; the warning of Esau.
kw: The whole upbringing of a child: teaching, training and correction. The word comes from pais, child.
Being made holy, set apart for God. Verse 10 says that God trains us so “that we may share his holiness”.
Profane, the opposite of holy: one who treats sacred things as common. Esau treated his birthright, the gift of God's promise, as worth one meal.
vv: for the Lord disciplines those whom he loves,
Proverbs 3:12. The discipline is the proof of the love, not its opposite.
Now, discipline always seems painful rather than pleasant at the time, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
“Trained” is an athletic word, gegymnasmenois, from which “gymnasium” comes. The fruit comes “later”.
See to it that no one becomes like Esau, an immoral and godless person, who sold his birthright for a single meal.
Genesis 25:29–34. Esau traded a lasting gift for a passing hunger. Verse 17 recalls his tears when the blessing went to Jacob (Genesis 27:34–38).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross: there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle, and spiritual progress involves discipline and self-denial that lead gradually to the peace and joy of the Beatitudes (CCC 2015). Verse 14, holiness “without which no one will see the Lord”, echoes the Beatitude of the pure in heart, who will see God (Matthew 5:8).

r.h: God, be merciful to me, a sinner
set: Luke says plainly to whom the parable is told: “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and regarded others with contempt” (18:9). Two men go up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee's practices go beyond what the Law required: the Law commanded fasting on the Day of Atonement, and he fasts twice a week; he tithes all he receives. What he says about himself is true. The trouble is the comparison and the contempt. The parable does not portray all Pharisees; it portrays a temptation that every devout person, Christians first of all, can fall into.
str: v. 9: to whom the parable is told.
vv. 10–12: the Pharisee's prayer.
v. 13: the tax collector's prayer.
v. 14: the verdict, and the saying about exalting and humbling.
kw: Treating others as nothing. This, more than his fasting, is what Jesus exposes.
A plea for atonement. The word is related to hilastērion, the mercy seat over the ark (Hebrews 9:5). He asks God to cover his sin.
Made right with God. It is God's verdict, not the man's own claim.
vv: God, I thank you that I am not like other people:
The prayer begins with thanks, but it is really about himself. He asks for nothing, and so receives nothing.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner!
He stands far off, does not look up, and beats his breast. His prayer is short and true. The Greek says “the sinner”, as if there were no other.
for all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but all who humble themselves will be exalted.
The same saying closes the parable of the places at table (14:11). In both, God is the one who lifts up.
ch: The Catechism calls humility the foundation of prayer (CCC 2559), and names this parable as the third of Luke's parables on prayer, the prayer of the humble heart (CCC 2613). The cry of the tax collector, joined with that of the blind men, lives on in the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern Churches, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners” (CCC 2667). In our Holy Qurbono the people answer again and again, “Kurielaison”, Lord, have mercy: the prayer of the tax collector on the lips of the whole Church.

qa: What does Hebrews mean when it says Esau “found no chance to repent”?

Genesis tells that Esau wept and begged for a blessing after Jacob had received it (Genesis 27:34–38). Many interpreters understand Hebrews to mean that he could not undo what was done: the birthright he had despised was gone, though his tears were real. Hebrews does not teach that God refuses a sinner who truly repents; the whole letter invites the readers to come near the throne of grace (4:16). It warns against trading a lasting gift for a passing appetite.
study: What hardship in my life might God be using to train me? Can I ask for the “peaceful fruit” it may bring?
When I pray, do I compare myself with others? Can I pray the tax collector's prayer slowly today?

lead: On the Fourth Sunday after Qyomtho every reading looks outward, from the empty tomb to the ends of the earth. The evening Gospel (Matthew 28:16–20) gives the great commission on the mountain in Galilee: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” Exodus 34:10–17 shows God renewing the covenant after the golden calf. Job 42:7–17 tells how the Lord restored Job when he prayed for the friends who had wronged him. In 1 Kings 3:4–15 the young Solomon asks for a listening heart and receives wisdom. In Acts 10:34–43 Peter learns in the house of Cornelius that “God shows no partiality”, and he says of the risen Lord, “We are witnesses.”

We study three readings more closely. Isaiah 49 promises a time of favour, when God's servant becomes a covenant for the people and the scattered come home from every direction. Paul tells the Corinthians that in Christ there is a new creation, and that God now makes his appeal through his ambassadors. In Luke the risen Lord shows his hands and feet, eats before his disciples, opens the Scriptures to them, and sends them to all nations. The key words are favour, reconciliation and witness.

r.h: In a time of favour I have answered you
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah are usually dated by scholars to the last years of the Babylonian exile, around 550–539 BC, when Cyrus of Persia was rising and a return home began to seem possible. They are often called Second Isaiah. The book itself opens this part with the word “Comfort, O comfort my people” (40:1), and today's reading closes on the same note.

Just before our passage stands the second of the four Servant Songs (49:1–6). There the Lord says to his servant: “I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (49:6). Verses 8–13 answer that song. The servant will lead a new exodus, and the road home will be easy because God himself prepares it.
str: v. 8: God answers and helps his servant and gives him as a covenant to the people.
v. 9a: the servant's word to the prisoners: come out into the light.
vv. 9b–11: the journey home: pasture, water, mountains turned into roads.
v. 12: the exiles return from every direction.
v. 13: heaven, earth and mountains are called to sing.
kw: A time when God is pleased to act. Paul quotes this verse in the Greek, and adds his own comment: “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The time of favour is not only a date in the past. It is today.

A bold phrase. The servant is not only the messenger of the covenant; he himself becomes the covenant, the bond between God and the people. The same words are used of the servant in 42:6. Christians hear in them the one whose blood is “the new covenant” (Luke 22:20).
The verb of 40:1, “Comfort, O comfort my people”. In v. 13 the comfort is no longer only promised. It has been given, and creation is invited to sing because of it.
vv: In a time of favor I have answered you, on a day of salvation I have helped you;
The verbs speak as if it were already done. God's promise is so sure that the prophet can describe it in the past tense.
saying to the prisoners, “Come out,” to those who are in darkness, “Show yourselves.”

The exiles were not in chains, but they were captives of a foreign empire and of their own despair. The command is to come out into the light. In Luke the risen Lord opens minds that had been closed by grief and fear (Luke 24:45).
Lo, these shall come from far away, and lo, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene.

Syene is Aswan in the far south of Egypt. Here the NRSV follows the great Isaiah scroll found at Qumran; the traditional Hebrew text has “Sinim”, a place no one has identified with certainty. Either way, the scattered come from every side.
For the Lord has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his suffering ones.
The word for compassion is related to the Hebrew for a mother's womb. The next verses make the picture plain: “Can a woman forget her nursing child?” (49:15).
ch: The Church has always read the Servant Songs in the light of Christ. Simeon sees in the child Jesus “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas take up Isaiah 49:6 as a command to themselves (Acts 13:47). Today's verses show the servant's work as a homecoming: prisoners brought out, the hungry fed, every road opened. That is the work the risen Lord gives to his witnesses in the Gospel, “to all nations”. The Catechism says that the Church's mission comes from the love of the Father, who wills that all be saved (CCC 849–851).

r.h: A new creation; ambassadors for Christ
set: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–57, after a painful break with the church he had founded in Corinth. Some there doubted him and preferred more impressive preachers. In chapters 2–7 he defends his ministry, and he does it by speaking of what God has done in Christ.

Just before today's verses Paul says that “the love of Christ urges us on”, because “one has died for all” (5:14). Since Christ died and was raised for all, no one can be seen any longer by worldly standards (5:16). Today's reading draws the conclusion.
str: v. 17: in Christ, a new creation.
vv. 18–19: all is from God, who reconciles the world to himself and gives the ministry of reconciliation.
v. 20: we are ambassadors; God makes his appeal through us.
v. 21: the exchange: the sinless one made sin, so that we might become God's righteousness.
¶ The appeal goes on at once in 6:1–2, where Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, today's Old Testament reading.
kw: The Greek has no verb: “if anyone in Christ: new creation!” The phrase looks back to the first creation and forward to the promise of “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). The new creation began in the risen body of Christ, and it reaches the believer through Baptism.

The word for making peace between two parties who had been estranged. Paul is careful: God is never the one who needs to be won over. It is God who reconciles us to himself, and the whole initiative is his. In Christ's sacrifice it is God himself who takes the initiative.
An ambassador speaks with the authority of the one who sends him, not his own. Paul's ministry is not his own message. It is God's appeal made through a human voice.
vv: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
The word “see” calls us to look. In Revelation the one seated on the throne says, “See, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).
All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation;
Two gifts in one sentence: the reconciliation itself, and the service of bringing it to others. The Church has the second only because she has first received the first.
So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
Paul writes this to people who are already baptized. Reconciliation is not a single moment. The baptized also need to hear again, “be reconciled to God”.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

One of the boldest sentences Paul wrote. Christ did not become a sinner. He took on himself the whole weight and result of our sin. Some Fathers, among them St Augustine, read “sin” here as “sacrifice for sin”, since the Old Testament could call a sin offering by the word for sin (in substance).
ch: The Catechism quotes 2 Corinthians 5:21 when it teaches that Christ died for our sins: Jesus was never a sinner himself, but in his redeeming love he took us upon himself in the state of our sin (CCC 602–603). It also takes the name of the sacrament of Reconciliation from verse 20, “Be reconciled to God” (CCC 1424), and teaches that Christ entrusted this ministry of reconciliation to his apostles and their successors (CCC 1442). Every Christian shares in the appeal. A baptized person who makes peace, forgives, and speaks of Christ is already an ambassador.

r.h: You are witnesses of these things
set: This is the last scene of Luke's Gospel before the Ascension. On Easter evening the two disciples have come back from Emmaus to tell how the Lord “had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread” (24:35). The eleven and their companions have their own news: “The Lord has risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). Our reading begins while they are still talking.

Luke wrote for readers who had never seen Jesus. He takes care to show that the risen Lord is no ghost and no mere memory, and that the mission of the Church flows from his own word. The same author continues the story in Acts, where the promise of verse 49 is fulfilled at Pentecost.
str: vv. 36–37: Jesus stands among them; their terror.
vv. 38–40: hands and feet: “it is I myself”.
vv. 41–43: he eats before them.
vv. 44–47: he opens their minds to the Scriptures: suffering, rising, preaching to all nations.
vv. 48–49: “You are witnesses”; the promise of the Father; wait in the city.
kw: The disciples think they are seeing a disembodied spirit. Jesus answers that “a ghost does not have flesh and bones”. The risen Lord is not less than a human body, but more.

A witness speaks of what he has seen and heard. The word will come to mean those who give their lives for that testimony. Peter uses it in today's reading from Acts: “We are witnesses to all that he did” (Acts 10:39).
The Holy Spirit, “what my Father promised”. Luke opens Acts with the same promise (Acts 1:4–8). The witnesses are not to go out in their own strength.
vv: Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”

The greeting is the ordinary Hebrew shalom, but on Easter evening it is a gift. Those who had abandoned him are greeted first with peace, not with reproach. A few ancient manuscripts leave out the greeting, but most have it, and John records the same words (John 20:19).
Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself.
The wounds are the proof of identity. The one who stands before them is the same one who was crucified, not another.
Have you anything here to eat?

A homely question. Their joy is so great that they cannot believe it, and he helps their faith with the plainest sign of a living body. Peter will later say they “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures,
The same Lord who opened the Scriptures on the road to Emmaus (24:27, 32) now opens the minds of the whole group. Understanding the Scriptures is his gift, given in his presence.
and that repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

The plan of Acts in one line: from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). Isaiah's servant was to be a light to the nations; the Lord now sends his disciples to carry that light.
You are witnesses of these things.
Not only of the empty tomb, but of all of it: the suffering, the rising, the Scriptures fulfilled, the forgiveness offered.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage to teach that the Resurrection was a real event and the risen body a real body: Jesus invites the disciples to see that he is not a ghost, and that his body is the same that was crucified, yet now with new properties of a glorious body (CCC 645). It also notes that the disciples were not credulous; their faith was born of an encounter they found hard to believe (CCC 643–644). Verse 47 is the root of the Church's preaching of repentance and forgiveness, and verse 49 of her waiting for the Spirit.

qa: Why did the risen Jesus keep his wounds?

The Gospels show that the wounds prove he is the same Jesus who was crucified. Christian tradition has also seen in them the signs of his love and of his victory over death. The Resurrection did not erase the Cross. It transformed it.
Does “all nations” mean the Gospel is against the old covenant with Israel?

No. Jesus says the preaching begins “from Jerusalem”, and he explains it from “the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms”. The mission to the nations fulfils God's promises to Israel, as Isaiah 49 shows. The Church confesses that God's gifts and call to the Jewish people are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).
Is every Christian really an “ambassador”?

Yes, in his or her own way. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the laity share in the mission of the whole Church through Baptism and Confirmation, and carry Christ into family, work and public life (Lumen Gentium 33; CCC 900). Priests have a particular ministry of reconciliation in the sacrament, but the appeal “be reconciled to God” is made through the life of every believer.
rite: Qyomtho is the Syriac word for resurrection, and our Church counts the Sundays of this season from Easter. Today is also the feast of St Mark the Evangelist, whose Gospel ends with the same sending to the whole creation. In the 2025–26 lectionary this Sunday was kept as Syro-Malankara Catholic Laity Day, and the readings still carry that note: the commission of Matthew 28, the witnesses of Luke 24 and the ambassadors of 2 Corinthians 5 are not only for clergy and religious. At the end of every Holy Qurbono the priest blesses the people and sends them out in peace. That blessing is a small Pentecost. We leave the altar as witnesses.
study: Where in my life does the risen Lord need to show me his hands and his feet, so that my doubts give way to joy?
Paul says that God makes his appeal through us. Whom do I know who most needs to hear “be reconciled to God”, and how might I say it?
Isaiah calls the servant “a covenant to the people”. How does the Holy Qurbono make that covenant present to us each Sunday?
Job was restored when he prayed for the friends who had wronged him. Whom should I pray for this week?

lead: Yesterday was the feast of St Mark, and today's Gospel comes from his book: the parable of the sower, which begins and ends with a call to listen. The Epistle tells us where God's word is now heard most fully. We have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The key words are come and listen.

r.h: You have come to Mount Zion
set: Hebrews is a long sermon in written form, addressed to Christians who were growing tired and tempted to fall back. Its author is unknown; the early Church already debated whether Paul wrote it. Chapter 12 urges the readers to run the race with their eyes on Jesus (12:1–2). Today's verses set two mountains side by side, Sinai, where the Law was given (Exodus 19–20; Deuteronomy 4–5), and Zion, the city of God.
str: vv. 18–21: what you have not come to: fire, darkness, trumpet, a voice no one could bear.
vv. 22–24: what you have come to: the city of the living God, angels, the firstborn, God, the righteous, Jesus and his blood.
kw: The verb is in a tense that speaks of arrival with lasting effect: you have come and you are here. It is also the word Hebrews uses for drawing near to God in worship (4:16; 10:22).
Ekklēsia is the word for the Church. The firstborn belonged to God in Israel (Exodus 13:2). Here all the faithful, “enrolled in heaven”, share that title in Christ, “the firstborn” (1:6).
The one who stands between two parties and binds them. Moses was mediator at Sinai; Jesus is mediator of the new covenant, and his own blood seals it (9:15).
vv: Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
These words are not found in the Sinai story of Exodus. They echo Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses fears God's anger after the golden calf. Even the great mediator of the old covenant trembled.
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,
The Christian is not waiting outside. In worship he is already joined to the festival of heaven, though still on the way.
and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
Abel's blood cried out from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10). The blood of Jesus speaks of mercy and forgiveness.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a description of her worship. The Second Vatican Council says that in the earthly liturgy we share in a foretaste of the heavenly liturgy celebrated in the holy city of Jerusalem, toward which we journey as pilgrims (Sacrosanctum Concilium 8; CCC 1090). The contrast is not between a cruel God and a kind one. The same God spoke at Sinai and speaks in his Son. What is new is that, through Jesus, the distance has been crossed.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: Mark gathers several parables in chapter 4. Jesus has already met growing opposition (3:6, 22) and has chosen the Twelve (3:13–19). Now he teaches from a boat, with the crowd on the shore. The explanation of the parable comes later, given to the disciples (4:13–20); today we hear the story as the crowd heard it.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: the boat, the crowd, teaching in parables.
vv. 3–8: the sower and four kinds of ground.
v. 9: the call to hear.
kw: Behind it is the Hebrew māshāl, which covers proverbs, riddles and stories. A parable draws the hearer in and leaves him to find the meaning, so it reveals to some and hides from others (4:11–12).
The parable opens with this command and closes with “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!” Israel's great prayer begins the same way: “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
vv: Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The sower scatters seed everywhere, even on the path and among stones. God does not first measure the soil before he speaks.
Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up quickly, since it had no depth of soil.
Quick growth is not the same as deep growth. Jesus later explains that these are people who receive the word with joy but fall away when trouble comes (4:16–17).
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
After three losses, a harvest beyond all expectation. Even Isaac's blessed harvest is called a hundredfold (Genesis 26:12). The parable ends in hope.
ch: The Church hears the parable as a call to examine the soil of the heart. The Catechism uses it to speak of the Kingdom: the word is like seed sown in a field, and those who hear it with faith have received the Kingdom itself (CCC 543). The Second Vatican Council quotes Jesus' saying that the word of the Lord is like a seed sown in a field (Lumen Gentium 5). For a family, the parable asks practical questions: what birds, rocks and thorns stop the word from growing in our home?

qa: Is the parable saying that some people are simply bad soil and cannot change?

No. A parable is a call, not a verdict. Jesus speaks so that the hearers will become good soil. The paths can be broken up, the stones removed and the thorns pulled out, and the grace of God is the farmer who does it with our consent.
study: Which of the four kinds of ground best describes how I heard last Sunday's word?
Hebrews says we have already come to the heavenly Jerusalem. How would I take part in the Holy Qurbono differently if I believed that?

lead: Today's readings ask what will remain when everything is shaken. Hebrews promises “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” and calls us to thank God for it. In Luke, a sincere ruler asks the way to eternal life, and finds that his wealth holds him more tightly than he knew. Peter's reply, “we have left our homes and followed you”, receives a promise. The key words are unshaken and follow.

r.h: A kingdom that cannot be shaken
set: These verses close the comparison between Sinai and Zion that began in 12:18. At Sinai God spoke on earth and the earth shook (Exodus 19:18). Now he speaks from heaven through his Son. Hebrews quotes the prophet Haggai, who promised after the exile that God would shake heaven and earth and fill his house with glory (Haggai 2:6–7).
str: v. 25: do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven.
vv. 26–27: the final shaking, which removes what is made and leaves what cannot be shaken.
vv. 28–29: so give thanks and worship with reverence, for God is a consuming fire.
kw: Used of the kingdom we are “receiving”. The present tense matters: the kingdom is being given now, and we are receiving it.
Literally “let us have grace” or “gratitude”. Thanksgiving is the right answer to a gift. The Greek word for thanksgiving, eucharistia, became the name of the Church's great act of worship.
vv: See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking;
God is still speaking. The danger is not that he is silent but that we turn away.
This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of what is shaken … so that what cannot be shaken may remain.
Everything made will be tested. What remains is what belongs to God's kingdom.
for indeed our God is a consuming fire.
Words from Deuteronomy 4:24. The fire that frightened Israel at Sinai is the same holy love that purifies and does not destroy what is true.
ch: The Church hears in verse 28 a description of the Holy Qurbono, the thanksgiving in which we receive the kingdom and offer “acceptable worship with reverence and awe”. The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 1359–1360). The fire of verse 29 is not something to run from. In the Syriac tradition the Holy Mysteries themselves are often called fire, which those who come in faith and reverence receive without harm.

r.h: One thing lacking
set: Luke places this meeting on Jesus' long journey to Jerusalem. Just before it, Jesus has blessed the little children and said that the kingdom must be received like a child (18:15–17). Only Luke calls the questioner a “ruler”, perhaps a leader in a synagogue or a man of standing. Matthew says he was young (Matthew 19:20). Mark adds that Jesus looked at him and loved him (Mark 10:21).
str: vv. 18–21: the question and the commandments.
vv. 22–23: “one thing lacking”; the ruler's sorrow.
vv. 24–27: the camel and the needle; what is possible for God.
vv. 28–30: Peter's word and Jesus' promise.
kw: A man with position as well as money. What he must leave is not only property but status.

The largest animal in the land and the smallest opening anyone could picture. The saying is a deliberate exaggeration. There is no good evidence for the popular story of a small gate in Jerusalem called “the needle's eye”.
Peter's words, translated “our homes” in the NRSV. The disciples had left their own boats, nets and families.
vv: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?

A good question asked sincerely. Jesus' reply, “No one is good but God alone”, is not a denial of his own goodness. It directs the man to the source of all goodness, the God who now stands before him.
There is still one thing lacking. Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.
The point of the command is the last words: “follow me”. The poor gain, and he gains treasure, but the real gift offered is Jesus himself.
What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.
Salvation is never a human achievement. Even letting go of what we cling to is a grace.
Then Peter said, “Look, we have left our homes and followed you.”
Peter is not boasting; he speaks for all who have left something for Jesus. The Lord's answer promises much more in this age and eternal life in the next.
ch: The Catechism uses this meeting to teach that the commandments are the first step on the way to eternal life, and that following Jesus is their fulfilment (CCC 2052–2053). The Church has never read the passage as a condemnation of all property. It calls every Christian to detachment, so that riches serve love of God and neighbour (CCC 2544–2547). Clement of Alexandria wrote a whole treatise, Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, to show that what must be given up is the soul's attachment to wealth (in substance).

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Cletus, also called Anacletus, Bishop of Rome. St Irenaeus names him as the successor of Linus, to whom the apostles Peter and Paul had entrusted the Church of Rome (Against Heresies III.3.3). Very little else is known of him. His memory reminds us that the faith reaches us through an unbroken line of shepherds, and that the Church of Rome, with which our Church is in full communion since 1930, has kept the apostles' teaching from the first generation.
study: What in my life do I hold so tightly that I would be sad if Jesus asked me to let it go?
Hebrews calls us to give thanks for an unshakable kingdom. For what will I thank God at the next Holy Qurbono?

lead: On the day the Panchangam remembers Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon, the Epistle begins, “Remember your leaders”, and the Gospel speaks of the servant whom the master puts in charge of his household. Both readings are about faithful service while the Lord seems to delay. Between them stands the sentence that holds every generation together: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The key words are remember and faithful.

r.h: Remember your leaders; we have an altar
set: Chapter 13 is the practical close of Hebrews: love of the brethren, hospitality, care for prisoners, faithfulness in marriage (13:1–6). Today's verses turn to the community's leaders, past and present, and then to worship. The readers seem to have been tempted by teachings about special foods, perhaps linked to the meals and rules of the old temple worship. Hebrews answers by pointing to Christ's sacrifice, offered outside the city.
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ is always the same.
vv. 9–10: not strange teachings about food: we have an altar.
vv. 11–14: the sin offering burned outside the camp; Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go out to him.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices of praise and of sharing.
kw: Those who go ahead and guide. The leaders of verse 7 have already finished their course; those of verse 17 are still watching over the readers. Both are to be honoured.
The place of sacrifice. Hebrews says that Christians are not people without an altar. The Fathers and the Church have read this verse of the altar of Christ's sacrifice and of the Eucharist.
A phrase from the Psalms (Psalm 50:14, 23). Praise and good works are called sacrifices because they are offered to God through Christ, the one high priest.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
Remembering is not nostalgia. It means looking at how they lived and ended, and copying their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders pass; the Lord they served does not. This is why the faith they handed on is still true for us.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.
On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). The Gospels agree that Jesus was crucified outside the city (John 19:17, 20).
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
The Christian is a pilgrim. This does not make him careless of the world; it leaves him ready to serve it.
ch: The Church has read “we have an altar” of the altar on which the one sacrifice of Christ is made present in the Eucharist (CCC 1365–1367). The sacrifices of praise and of sharing in verses 15–16 flow from that altar into daily life; they do not replace it. The Catechism teaches that the Church prays for the faithful departed, and above all offers the Eucharistic sacrifice for them (CCC 1032). So on this day we remember a shepherd of our Church, thank God for him, and pray for his rest.

r.h: The faithful and wise servant
set: Chapters 24–25 of Matthew are Jesus' last great discourse, spoken on the Mount of Olives a few days before his death. He speaks of the end of the temple and of his coming at the end of the age. Since no one knows the day or the hour (24:36), the discourse turns to a series of parables about readiness. Today's follows the short saying about the thief in the night (24:43–44); tomorrow's parable of the ten bridesmaids comes next.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise servant?
vv. 46–47: the blessing of the servant found at work.
vv. 48–51: the wicked servant who says, “My master is delayed”.
kw: Faithful means reliable when no one is watching; wise means seeing what really matters. The same word for “wise” describes the bridesmaids who took oil (25:2).
The servant's excuse. The same verb is used of the bridegroom in the next parable (25:5). The early Church knew the experience of waiting, and Jesus teaches that the delay is a time for faithfulness.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The servant is a steward over fellow servants. The Fathers often applied the parable to bishops and priests, who are to feed God's household with the word and the sacraments.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The blessing is not for one who calculates the date, but for one found doing his ordinary task.
and he begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with drunkards,
When the master seems far away, authority turns into abuse. Jesus warns those who serve that their office is a trust, not a possession.
ch: The Church reads the parable first as a word to all who hold office in her. The Second Vatican Council describes the bishop as one sent to serve and to feed the flock, after the example of the Good Shepherd (Lumen Gentium 27). It is also a word to every Christian, for each of us has been put in charge of something: a family, a work, a gift. The strong ending in verse 51 is Matthew's way of saying how serious it is to betray such a trust.

qa: Why do we pray for bishops and priests who have died?

Because the Church prays for all the faithful departed. Even holy shepherds may need purification before they see God, and our prayer, above all the Holy Qurbono, helps them (CCC 1030–1032). To pray for them is also to thank God for what we received through them.
rite: Today the Panchangam keeps the memory of Most Rev. Isaac Mar Yoohanon, a bishop of our Church, who entered his rest in 1987. It also offers John 10:11–18, John 14:1–6 or John 15:9–17 as Gospels that may be read on this memory. In our tradition the names of the departed shepherds are remembered in the Holy Qurbono, and Hebrews 13:7 tells us why: their faith is a lamp for ours.
study: Who first spoke the word of God to me? How can I imitate their faith this week?
What has the Lord put me in charge of? Would he find me at work if he came today?

lead: Paul's short blessing for the Thessalonians asks that the whole person be kept ready “at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”, and adds a promise: “The one who calls you is faithful.” The Gospel tells of ten bridesmaids waiting through the night for the bridegroom, and of the oil that cannot be borrowed at the last moment. The Panchangam also remembers St Catherine of Siena, a woman of prayer whose lamp burned brightly in a dark time. The key words are ready and faithful.

r.h: May the God of peace sanctify you entirely
set: 1 Thessalonians is very probably the oldest writing of the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51 to a young church he had to leave in a hurry (Acts 17:1–10). The readers had questions about the Lord's coming and about members who had died (4:13–5:11). Today's verses are the letter's closing blessing and greetings.
str: v. 23: the prayer: holiness of the whole person until the Lord's coming.
v. 24: the promise: God who calls is faithful.
vv. 25–26: “pray for us”; the holy kiss.
kw: Complete, through and through. Paul prays that no part of life be left outside God's holiness.

Paul is not giving a lesson in how a person is made, but naming the whole human being. The Catechism explains that “spirit” here signifies that man is ordered from his creation to a supernatural end (CCC 367).
The word for the visit of a king. In the New Testament it is the Lord's coming in glory.
vv: May the God of peace himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be kept sound and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Holiness reaches the body too. That is why the Church cares for the body: in fasting and feasting, in chastity, in care for the sick, in reverence for the dead.
The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.
The whole of Christian hope rests here. We do not make ourselves holy; God who began the work will finish it, if we let him.
Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.
An early sign of peace among believers. The Church's liturgies kept it in the kiss of peace.
ch: The Catechism takes verse 23 to explain the unity of body and soul: the distinction of soul and spirit does not make two souls in man (CCC 367). Verse 24 grounds the Christian virtue of hope, which rests not on our strength but on God's faithfulness to his promises (CCC 1817). For a West Syriac Christian the holy kiss is familiar: in the Holy Qurbono the peace is passed from the altar to the people at the beginning of the anaphora, as a sign that we come to the offering reconciled.

r.h: Look! Here is the bridegroom!
set: This parable of readiness, spoken on the Mount of Olives, comes straight after yesterday's faithful servant. It reflects a village wedding: the bridegroom came, often at night, to bring the bride to his home, and young women went out with lights to join the procession. The exact customs are not fully known, but the picture was clear to Jesus' hearers. The Old Testament prophets had already called God the bridegroom of his people (Hosea 2:19–20; Isaiah 62:5).
str: vv. 1–4: ten bridesmaids; five take oil, five do not.
vv. 5–7: the delay, the sleep, the midnight shout.
vv. 8–9: the request for oil and the refusal.
vv. 10–12: the door shut; “I do not know you”.
v. 13: “Keep awake therefore”.
kw: Unmarried young women of the bride's or groom's circle. The NRSV calls them bridesmaids. The Fathers often saw in them the whole Church, waiting for Christ.
Perhaps torches whose rags were soaked in oil, which would burn only a short time without a supply. Hence the need for flasks.
Not “do not sleep”, since all ten slept. It means: be ready, so that when the call comes you can rise and go out.
vv: but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.
The difference between them is not seen at first. All have lamps, all go out, all sleep. It shows only when the bridegroom comes.
But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’
The hour no one expects. The cry is joyful: the waiting is over.
But the wise replied, ‘No! there will not be enough for you and for us; you had better go to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’
This is not selfishness. Some things cannot be handed over at the last moment: no one can believe, love or be ready for another.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
The lesson of the whole discourse in one line.
ch: St Augustine asked what the oil means and answered that it is charity, love that is hidden within and keeps the lamp burning (Sermon 93, in substance). The Catechism quotes the Council's call to watch constantly, since we know neither the day nor the hour, so that we may enter with the Lord into the marriage feast (CCC 1036; Lumen Gentium 48). The parable is serious, but its centre is joy: a bridegroom, a feast, a door opened to those who are ready.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), virgin and Doctor of the Church. A laywoman of the Dominican order, she gave herself to prayer and to the sick and poor of her city, and she worked for the return of the Pope from Avignon to Rome and for peace in the Church. Her Dialogue is a classic of Christian prayer. Her life fits today's Gospel: her biographer, Bl. Raymond of Capua, tells of her mystical espousal to Christ, and she kept her lamp burning to the end.
study: What is the “oil” in my lamp, and how do I keep it supplied day by day?
Paul prays for the sanctifying of spirit, soul and body. Which of these do I most neglect in my life with God?

lead: On the feast of Mar Yaqob Shleeha, St James the son of Zebedee, the Gospel shows him before he understood: asking with his brother John for the seats of honour, and hearing instead of a cup and a baptism. Jesus promised, “The cup that I drink you will drink”, and James became the first of the Twelve to die for him (Acts 12:2). The Epistle from Galatians shows what greatness looks like in a community formed by that cup: restoring the fallen gently, bearing one another's burdens, and not growing weary in doing good. The key words are cup, serve and restore.

r.h: Bear one another's burdens
set: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia, in the interior of what is now Turkey, when some teachers were urging his Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic law in order to belong fully to God's people. Paul's answer fills the letter: we are made right with God through faith in Christ, and the Spirit has been given to us (3:1–5). The date is uncertain; many place it in the early or middle 50s.

Chapter 5 has set the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit (5:16–26). Today's verses show what life in the Spirit looks like in ordinary church life. Paul is not speaking of a vague goodwill but of concrete care: for the one who falls, for the teacher, for all, and especially for “the family of faith”.
str: v. 1: restore the one who has fallen, gently, watching yourself.
vv. 2–5: bear one another's burdens; test your own work; carry your own load.
v. 6: share good things with those who teach you.
vv. 7–8: you reap what you sow: flesh or Spirit.
vv. 9–10: do not grow weary; do good to all.
kw: A word used of setting a broken bone or mending nets. Mark uses it of James and John themselves, “in their boat mending the nets” when Jesus called them (Mark 1:19). The fishermen of Galilee became menders of people.

Two different words. The baros of v. 2 is a heavy weight that one person cannot carry alone, so others must help. The phortion of v. 5 is one's own pack, the responsibility no one else can take. Paul holds both together.
Used in vv. 9 and 10: the harvest will come in its own time, and meanwhile “whenever we have an opportunity”, we are to do good. God's time and our chance are the same word.
vv: if anyone is detected in a transgression, you who have received the Spirit should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.
The test of a spiritual person is not that he never sees sin in others, but how he handles it: with gentleness, which is part of the fruit of the Spirit (5:23).
Bear one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

Paul has argued against putting Gentiles under the Mosaic law. Yet Christians are not lawless. The law of Christ is the love that he showed, summed up in 5:14: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Do not be deceived; God is not mocked, for you reap whatever you sow.
A farmer's proverb. What we give our life to will grow. God's grace does not cancel this; it makes it possible to sow to the Spirit.
So let us not grow weary in doing what is right, for we will reap at harvest time, if we do not give up.
Good done in secret and without thanks is not lost. The harvest is God's, and it comes in his time.
let us work for the good of all, and especially for those of the family of faith.
The circle of love reaches everyone, and has a centre: the household of believers. The two are not rivals.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a rule of fraternal life. The Catechism speaks of fraternal correction as a work of charity (CCC 1829), and the Church's practice of correction is meant to heal and restore, never to humiliate. Bearing one another's burdens is the root of the works of mercy (CCC 2447). Verse 8 does not teach that we earn eternal life by our own power. We sow to the Spirit by grace, and the life we reap is God's gift; the Council of Trent teaches that eternal life is both a grace and a reward promised by God to good works done in Christ (CCC 2006–2011 in substance).

r.h: Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, walking ahead of his frightened disciples (10:32). He has just foretold his Passion for the third time, in the fullest detail: he will be handed over, condemned, mocked, flogged and killed, and after three days he will rise (10:33–34). At once James and John ask for the places of honour. Mark sets the two scenes side by side so that we feel the distance between the Lord's mind and theirs.

James and John were among the first four disciples called (1:16–20). With Peter they saw the raising of Jairus' daughter (5:37), the Transfiguration (9:2) and the agony in Gethsemane (14:33). Jesus named them “Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder” (3:17). Matthew tells the same scene but has their mother make the request (Matthew 20:20–21).
str: vv. 35–37: the request for the right and the left.
vv. 38–40: the cup and the baptism; the places are not Jesus' to grant.
v. 41: the anger of the ten.
vv. 42–44: not so among you: the great must serve.
v. 45: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life a ransom for many.
kw: In the Old Testament the cup can mean the portion God gives, of blessing (Psalm 23:5; 116:13) or of judgment and suffering (Isaiah 51:17). Here it is the cup of the Passion. In Gethsemane Jesus will pray, “remove this cup from me” (14:36).
From the verb for plunging or immersing. Jesus speaks of being plunged into suffering and death. Luke records a similar saying: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized” (Luke 12:50).

The price paid to set a captive or slave at liberty. Jesus does not explain to whom the price is paid; he says what it costs and what it achieves. The phrase “for many” echoes the Servant of Isaiah 53:11–12, who bears the sins of many.
vv: Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.

They believe he will reign, and that is to their credit. What they do not yet see is the throne he goes to. Mark will later show who are at his right and his left in that hour: two bandits on crosses (15:27).
You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?
Jesus does not rebuke them harshly. He leads them from the thought of honour to the thought of sharing his suffering.
The cup that I drink you will drink;

A prophecy fulfilled for James in Jerusalem around AD 44, when Herod Agrippa I “had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword” (Acts 12:2). John drank the cup by long witness and suffering for Christ.
But it is not so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant,
Jesus does not forbid authority in his community. He changes its meaning: authority becomes service.
For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.
The key to the whole Gospel of Mark. The one who will come on the clouds with power (Daniel 7:13–14) first comes to serve and to die.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus willingly offered his life as “a ransom for many”, and that “many” is not restrictive: it sets the whole of humanity over against the one Redeemer who gives himself (CCC 605; see 622). It also says that ministry in the Church is by its nature service, after the pattern of Christ who made himself the servant of all (CCC 876). St John Chrysostom notes that the Lord did not scold the brothers, but led them gently from the request for honour to the cup (in substance). James learned the lesson, and the Church honours him as the first apostle to give his life for Christ.

qa: Which James is this?

James the son of Zebedee, brother of John, sometimes called James the Greater. He is not the same as James the son of Alphaeus, another of the Twelve (Mark 3:18), nor the same as “James the brother of the Lord”, who still led the church in Jerusalem after the son of Zebedee had been put to death (Galatians 1:19; Acts 12:2; 15:13).
Was the request of James and John simply ambition?

Partly, and Jesus corrects it. But it was also faith: they believed he would come into his glory when others saw only danger ahead. Jesus does not reject them. He promises them a share in his cup, and he keeps that promise.
Does Galatians 6:5 contradict 6:2?

No. Paul uses two different words. Some burdens are too heavy for one person, and the community must carry them together. Others belong to each person, like conscience and our own account before God. A healthy Christian community does both: it helps, and it does not take away each person's responsibility.
rite: Our Church keeps today the feast of Mar Yaqob Shleeha. Shleeha is the Syriac word for apostle, one who is sent. The Byzantine Churches also honour St James the son of Zebedee on this day, while the Latin Church keeps his feast on 25 July. He is the only apostle whose martyrdom is recorded in the New Testament. In the Holy Qurbono we drink from the cup that Jesus spoke of in this Gospel, and we are reminded that sharing his cup means sharing his life of service. As we receive the Holy Mysteries today, we ask Mar Yaqob to pray that we may be able to drink it as he did.
study: If Jesus asked me, “What is it you want me to do for you?”, what would I honestly answer?
What “cup” has the Lord given me to drink at this time in my life? How can I drink it with him?
Whom in my family or parish might I restore “in a spirit of gentleness” rather than judge?
Where am I growing weary in doing good? What would help me not to give up?
